items.body: Footfalls (Miasmah, November 22) is a collaboration between Gareth Davis and Scanner. The pair present two scenes, loosely inspired by the poets and novelists T.S Elliot and Samuel Beckett and taken from differing sides of the same desolate seaside setting. In the grip of winter, the seaside slants, becoming bleak, and it’s a sharp contrast from an endless summer, with lifeless, empty harbours and thick clumps of seaweed hanging from the crests of cold waves. The water temperature has dropped to that of ice in liquid form. This desolation manifests through a bass clarinet – played by Gareth Davis – and its long, slinking drone stretches the music, causing it to echo through a rainy day and along soggy sand. Tourists don’t see this side of the beach, and the music reflects this. As ever, Scanner (Robin Rimbaud) provides an impressive range of electronic oscillations and manipulations. Sound waves ride shotgun on their own tides, pulsing and then falling back, bubbling up and receding into nothingness, sometimes bringing the staccato of dashes and dots, and other times shrouding the clarinet’s tone in an electronic-made fog that comes rolling off the ocean, pulsing, glowing. John Carpenter would be proud. The sharp synths that enter seven or so minutes into the eighteen-minute opener ‘Towards The Door’ cut through the electronics, coming out of nowhere and rising up over the cold beach. The wail of a siren. The change in register lifts the music up, even if it’s just a temporary perch, and there’s no forewarning to it, which increases the sense of unease. For the most part, it remains low, stuck in the gloom of an overcast day, dank and grey. This won’t appear on the postcards when summer season rolls around. Towards the end, the artificial sounds of the sea bleed out, and the authentic sound of the sea’s waves replace the electronic waves via field recordings of the ocean. Although the lapping of the shore is calming and ambient (Eno didn’t create ambient music – nature did), frequently used in meditation and rest, it feels a little cooler here, a little disquieting. The whole piece is mesmerising. ‘Smokefall’ is more voice-oriented, as it repeats and distorts a running phrase. Like some kind of nightmarish mantra, the voice lies in the background, barely audible, a radio signal or a police band picked up by an amplifier and hijacked by accident. The electronics are more jagged here, providing a scratchy rhythm of their own: we’ve gone past the seafront and now stand beside the cliffs, walking around the top of the promenade for a better view…although it’s still largely the same, a grey, rolling mass covering the entire horizon. Environments affect the mind and its emotional tides, positively, negatively, or nonchalantly, and this bank of water does little to lift the tonal depression. Although the bass clarinet has more of a range and chooses to move around a bit more, it’s still not overly flexible, and the electronics wrap it up, constricting it. In fact, Scanner’s electronics are central to this piece. Although prolific, these two musicians never seem to run out of ideas. Footfalls is another step in the right direction. www.miasmah.com
items._genre: ambient / drone / experimental electronic / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由低音单簧管演奏家Gareth Davis与电子音乐人Scanner合作，以T.S.艾略特和贝克特的文学意象为底色，描绘冬季海滨的荒凉与孤寂。Davis的低音单簧管拉出一条绵长蜿蜒的持续低音，像雾气一样笼罩在阴冷的海滩上；Scanner的电子振荡与处理则构建出潮汐般的声波起伏，有时让单簧管的音色陷入电子迷雾之中。十八分钟的开篇曲目后半段由电子海浪过渡为真实的海滩田野录音，将人造声响与自然环境融合。第二首作品转向人声采样，将一段循环短语反复扭曲变形，如噩梦般的咒语，电子部分也变得更加尖锐粗粝。专辑由挪威小厂牌Miasmah发行，低沉、灰暗、阴冷但不放弃对美的追寻。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国裔肯尼亚鼓手Sven Kacirek与双人组合Odd Okoddo的核心成员Olith Ratengo共同制作，并邀请八十三岁的传统肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo参与录制。音乐以Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手鼓和偶尔的架子鼓为骨架，承载人声的表达，同时保留了东肯尼亚dodo传统的深度。评论特别分析了'Bara'一曲中合成器多节奏层叠的微妙构建过程，以及'Sarah'中电子扭曲与人声张力之间的呼应。整篇文章关注的焦点在于这种跨文化合作如何让传统根源与前卫电子手法相互渗透，形成一种既全球化又深植非洲本土的当代声响，同时也提及了类似Chouk Bwa与Nyege Nyege厂牌的音乐场景。

items.body: Bracaloni’s latest traverse moves through warm, spacious soundscapes built for getting lost within, where atmosphere lingers long after each piece fades. A surreal sonic collage of ambient electronics Stars are Crashing, Home are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet by Fallen   Like a shield of emotive melodic strands gathering before our eyes, Lorenzo Bracaloni’s Fallen project shifts through time and space, blending ethereal voices with instrumental electronica across the long-winded (but apropo) Touched Music title, Stars are Crashing, Homes are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet. Fifteen slices of life unfold through ambient propulsion, opening with cascading sonic beauty on “Rusted Gardens,” where pitter-patter patterns breathe against a spacious atmosphere, quietly revealing how essential sound can be. Bracaloni’s signature drifts into darker territory with “Violent Winds,” yet remains light and airy, its floating voices drawing us deeper into a mesmerizing current. Downtempo bubbles and understated beatwork provide a gentle respite on “Wide Red Skies.” These are tranquil, ethereal spaces where music opens pathways rather than directing the listener. “The Vanishing,” “Hearts are Changing,” “Chasing Mechanical Butterflies,” and “From Dry Iron Valleys to Utopian Realms” could each have formed the core of a powerful extended player, while closing piece “Direction Home (Ruins Pathway)” ignites something deeper, allowing everything that came before to drift into one surreal sonic collage of ambient electronics, emotional textures, and shifting plateaus. Early heavyweight ambient/IDM artists such as Arovane, Biosphere, and Global Communication, alongside cinematic world-builders like Yagya, Secede, and Deepchord / Echospace, will find familiar connections throughout. As a result, Bracaloni’s latest traverse moves through warm, spacious soundscapes built for getting lost within, where atmosphere lingers long after each piece fades. Stars are Crashing, Homes are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet is available on Touched Music. items._cn_summary: Lorenzo Bracaloni 以 Fallen 之名推出的这张专辑包含十五首曲目，横跨温暖而宽广的声景空间。作品以级联式音画开场，将空灵人声与器乐电子交织，氛围在曲目消散后仍持久留存。文本描述其音乐质地轻盈漂浮，在下沉拍与节制节奏中留出呼吸余地，轨道之间形成超现实的声波拼贴。多首作品展现出独立成为延长播放核心的潜力，尾曲则将前序元素汇聚融合。评论提及与 Arovane、Biosphere、Global Communication 等早期氛围与智能舞曲先驱的渊源，并关联 Yagya、Secede、Deepchord 等具有电影感的世界构建者。整体定位为适合迷失其中的氛围电子作品，强调声音作为通径而非指令的体验。

items.body: Distort Everything Forever opens in ambience, spends most of its middle throwing rhythmic and low frequency chaos at you, then returns toward atmosphere at the end. The record opens a door, destroys the room, then leaves you in the wreckage Distort Everything Forever by SUAHN   SUAHN is Michael York, Baltimore-based, and his music has been moving through bass music, acid, techno, jungle, and experimental club forms long enough that Distort Everything Forever doesn’t arrive sounding like a debut. York grew up hearing hand-me-down mix CDs from his uncle, Aphex Twin and Venetian Snares sitting next to The Cure and Bauhaus on the same tape. That detail explains a lot about the harsher edges of what he makes. Four Tet, RL Grime, Ivy Lab, and Boombox Cartel have all picked up his catalog. He appeared on VISION‘s MISSION 03 compilation alongside Billain, Posij, Current Value, and others. So the full-length context is already there before a single track plays. The opener “Reverie” starts in ambience. Gives the impression things might unfold slowly. That doesn’t last. Heavy bass, drum and bass breaks, distorted percussion, hip hop rhythmic ideas, it arrives fast and stays physical for most of the runtime. York doesn’t spend time introducing himself. The drums show up and the record commits. The title is a literal description of the production language. Distortion isn’t decoration here, it bleeds into everything. Drums, bass, breaks, vocal fragments, transitional material. At a certain point it stops being an effect and becomes the identity of the record. There’s drum and bass underneath a lot of this, but also half-time hip hop programming, bass music, and the heavier side of experimental club production. Points where it touches the same territory as VISION releases—beat-driven material where drum and bass structure gets slowed, stretched apart, and rebuilt around enormous low end. “Drifting” is where the album properly declares itself. Old school drum and bass instinct in the way it moves. Not especially melodic, doesn’t need to be. The drums do most of the talking. Filter sweeps and frequency movement pull you further in gradually, and York trusts the breaks to establish the personality of the track without constantly dropping another melodic idea on top. That restraint is what makes the track land. “Lost in it All” goes heavier. Half-time rhythms, bass with real dub-like weight, distortion threatening to tear it apart at the edges. This is where the VISION comparison becomes most useful, the heavier beat-focused side of NOISIA‘s label, where sound design carries as much importance as composition and a bass hit functions almost like a lead instrument. York understands that language. The saturation and distortion give his version a dirtier edge than most producers working in that space would allow. The tracks sound filthy because they’re supposed to :: Worth noting what heavy distortion actually costs at the mix stage. Once you start saturating bass, drums, and midrange simultaneously, everything generates additional harmonics that compete for the same frequency space. Transients lose definition. Low mids turn to mud. The challenge is making something sound destroyed while still giving every important element enough room to be understood. York handles this well, the tracks sound filthy because they’re supposed to, but the kicks still hit, the bass still has shape, and the breaks never collapse into an undefined wall of noise. That kind of control doesn’t happen accidentally. “How Dark it Gets” is another standout, specifically for the vocal work. Fragments getting chopped, repositioned, distorted, thrown against the breaks, the edits never become a gimmick because they function as another rhythmic layer. Small pieces surface, disappear, return processed differently. The track feels like it’s constantly rearranging itself while you’re inside it. What becomes clear across the full runtime is how studied York is in this corner of electronic music. The Aphex Twin and Venetian Snares references from his background make sense, but this isn’t an IDM record in the older Warp or Rephlex sense. The center of gravity is heavier, connected to modern bass production, jungle, drum and bass, industrial club music, and the post-NOISIA school of extremely controlled sound design. Someone who understands what happens when breaks become texture, when distortion becomes arrangement, when bass stops functioning as low end and starts carrying the emotional weight of a track. The sequencing does real work too. Distort Everything Forever opens in ambience, spends most of its middle throwing rhythmic and low frequency chaos at you, then returns toward atmosphere at the end. The quiet at the beginning and the quiet at the end aren’t the same quiet. Everything that happened between them changes what the stillness means. The record opens a door, destroys the room, then leaves you in the wreckage. That’s a complete thought. Distort Everything Forever is available on Bandcamp. Distort Everything Forever by SUAHNThe post SUAHN :: Distort Everything Forever (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Terrifying Angels by Pure Reason Revolution sees the band making their darkest and heaviest album to date, but still keeping specific musical quirks that the band are known for. Taking their new prog sound into elements that include dark ambient, nu metal, psychedelic, symphonic and alternative rock, it proves that Jon Courtney's project still has heavy weight and impression. The trade off of vocals between Courtney & Annicke Shireen are mixed perfectly, with great depth and tone, while musically the band explore all aspects of their sound, making this a true stand out in their discography. While the longer tracks are the true attention grabbers, the shorter songs do keep to their more classic sound with heavier elements. I'd give this a low to mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Terrifying Angels.

items.body: Then Comes Silence have reached a point where the more interesting question is no longer whether they have an identifiable sound, but what they are prepared to do with an identity that has become so clearly their own. Formed in Stockholm in 2012 and operating since 2022 as the trio of Alex Svenson, Hugo Zombie and Jonas Fransson, the band are now approaching their eighth album, “Requiem Ballroom,” due on 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records. Conceived as a diptych, the record divides itself between Requiem and Ballroom, darkness and light, while recent singles “Judgement Day” and “Remaker Redeemer” have already begun to expose the contrast between those two halves. When I spoke with the band in 2024, our conversation touched on originality, conformity and the peculiar conservatism that can develop inside a scene supposedly built around difference. Two years later, those questions have become even more relevant. Rather than discussing “Requiem Ballroom” track by track, we returned to the larger tensions around it: how a band changes without performing reinvention for its own sake, when identity becomes formula, whether nostalgia can disguise itself as tradition, what happens when a trio becomes more focused by becoming smaller, and why sustaining a life in music may now be a harder problem than sustaining an artistic identity. Then Comes Silence interview Karo: When we spoke in 2024, Alex, you said the dark scene develops slowly and needs more originality. Two years later, Then Comes Silence are still immediately recognisable. How do you distinguish a strong identity from a language that has simply become comfortable? Alex: I still think the dark scene is developing very slowly. Can you honestly hear much of a difference between 2019 and 2026? The sound is basically the same, and most of the melodies still follow the same structures. I don’t know what others say about us, but I do think we distinguish ourselves from much of the scene by focusing more on the songs than on the sound. In that sense, we work in a rather traditional way: intro, verse, bridge and chorus. But who am I to judge? If people want to hear the same snare drum, synth pads and chorus-soaked guitars over and over again, maybe that’s what makes them feel good. I just know that we, Then Comes Silence, don’t really think that way. Karo: Your music has never depended on radical stylistic reinvention. Do you think artistic development can happen through changes in proportion, tension and emphasis rather than through introducing obviously new genres or sounds? Hugo: I think it can be a bit of everything you mention. We mix elements of different genres, such as that euro disco synth on “Judgement Day,” and this time we even tried new, exotic instruments in the recording. Both act as new ingredients in the Then Comes Silence sound. But just like a pizza, you can add different toppings and it will still be a pizza. Karo: “Requiem Ballroom” is built around opposites: darkness and light, ending and renewal. Yet Then Comes Silence have often been most interesting in the spaces between opposites: melody and severity, electronics and physical rock instrumentation, melancholy and momentum. Is the album’s binary structure something you actually believe in, or something you wanted to test and complicate? Alex: We believe in everything we do. There’s no theatre. This album is an experiment and a game. Team this vs team that. Karo: The two halves were mixed separately, by Tom van Heesch and Jon Bordon, but still have to exist as one Then Comes Silence record. Where does the identity of the band ultimately reside if the same material can be viewed through two different sonic perspectives? Hugo: The two halves were mixed separately, and recorded differently: different drums, amps, guitars. We wanted them both to have a distinct sound, but at the same time we didn’t want the album to feel like a compilation, so there’s still a sense of coherence between them. The identity of the band is there because it’s the same band using different approaches. Karo: Since becoming a trio, the band has sounded increasingly focused rather than reduced. Has having fewer people in the room actually widened the musical possibilities because the core identity became clearer? Hugo: It’s easier to work with a smaller team of totally focused people than a bigger team that includes distracted people with other priorities. That will only slow you down. Our roles in the band are totally clear; we are all focused on what we are doing, and that allows us to be more effective. Karo: You have now reached your eighth album. At this stage, is reinvention still a useful ambition, or does it become more interesting to understand more precisely what Then Comes Silence should never lose? Alex: We have been constantly active for years and haven’t really taken a break from each other or from music. The soul of Then Comes Silence will always stay the same, no matter how many times we reinvent ourselves. Karo: In our previous conversation, you spoke very positively about the Goth and Post-Punk community but also criticised its tendency towards conformity. Now that Then Comes Silence themselves are an established part of that scene, is it harder to criticise its conventions from the inside? Hugo: We all love the Goth and Post-Punk community. It’s our home. But I don’t think it matters how established you are; conformity will always be the enemy of creativity, which is meant to be at the core of this scene. For me, there are a lot of bands using the same formula, and it feels boring. But then again, others could think that we are doing the same, so in the end it doesn’t really matter. It’s just about what you enjoy listening to and what you don’t. Karo: You also mentioned then that younger audiences in the US gave you hope for the future of the scene. Two years and a great deal of touring later, do you still see a generational difference in how people approach Goth and Post-Punk, or has that picture become more complicated? Hugo: We are starting to notice more youngsters in the audience in Europe too. And that’s amazing. Precisely here in Stockholm we have a really nice and growing scene of young people making music, DJing, going to shows, and that’s great to see. Karo: A band with a long catalogue eventually develops an unwritten contract with its audience: there are sounds, songs and emotional qualities people expect. Do those expectations ever become creatively restrictive, or can they provide a useful resistance to work against? Alex: We’re always prepared to get caked by disappointed fans. We still get comments from people who miss a fourth member to fill the void of a second guitar. Thankfully, we’re in good company. The large majority of our followers are right there with us. Wherever we go, they follow. And wherever they point, we go. Karo: Then Comes Silence have always drawn from older Goth and Post-Punk traditions without sounding like a historical reconstruction. As that original musical history moves further into the past, what makes the difference between inheritance and nostalgia for you? Hugo: I think that we’re definitely not a nostalgia band. We don’t try to sound retro. But we listen to a lot of different genres, and most of the music we listen to is old. I mean, we are not trying to sound like Sisters of Mercy, The Mission or Lords of the New Church, but we probably have the same influences they had back then. Karo: The imagery surrounding “Requiem Ballroom” revolves around symbolic death, transformation and renewal. After more than a decade as a band, does the idea of renewal mean something different now than it would have when Then Comes Silence began in 2012? Alex: No, the only differences would be practical ones. A new instrument, new effects pedals, or a new producer behind the mix. The artistic renewal will always come from within. Karo: Looking beyond this album, what question about Then Comes Silence remains unresolved for you? What are you still trying to understand about this band that eight albums have not answered yet? Alex: Artistically, I have no comments and no expectations about what’s to come. I feel no anxiety about the music, and I don’t really care what other people say. But on the other hand, I’m trying to understand why we can’t make a living from what we do, and why it’s so difficult to reach a wider audience. The inflation affecting everyone on this planet doesn’t seem to apply to artists. People still don’t want to pay more for a show ticket, while they seem willing to pay twice as much for gas, milk or eggs in the store. Touring artists are facing higher and higher expenses, and many of them would probably need to cancel shows just to make ends meet. But they don’t, because there simply aren’t any realistic alternatives for live music. It must be even harder for the new young generation of musicians. I can’t see why it wouldn’t be. I’m trying to understand it, but I still haven’t found a good answer. About Then Comes Silence Then Comes Silence were formed in Stockholm in 2012 by vocalist, bassist and keyboard player Alex Svenson. Drummer Jonas Fransson joined in 2015, followed by guitarist Hugo Zombie in 2018; since 2022, the band have operated as a three-piece. Their discography has moved through labels including Novoton, Nuclear Blast, SPV and Metropolis Records, while extensive touring has taken them across Europe, North America and, in 2026, Latin America. Their eighth studio album, “Requiem Ballroom,” will be released on 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records. Structured as two contrasting halves, Requiem and Ballroom, the album uses darkness and light not simply as visual motifs but as different approaches to arrangement and production. The current singles are “Judgement Day” and “Remaker Redeemer,” with the latter introducing the Ballroom side and its themes of rebirth, cleansing and beginning again.

items.body:
A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. A former member of The Lounge Lizards and Levon Helm’s Midnight Ramble Band, Bernstein has also composed works for film, theater, and dance in addition to doing arrangements for a diverse list of artists, including Lou Reed, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Allen Toussaint, Marianne Faithfull, Linda Ronstadt, Rufus Wainwright, Darlene Love, Mario Pavone, Bill Frisell, and John Lurie. His lengthy list of sideman credits includes appearances on recent recordings by Laurie Anderson (Heart of a Dog), Roswell Rudd (Trombone for Lovers), Mostly Other People Do the Killing (Loafer’s Hollow), Antony and the Johnsons (Turning), and Nels Cline (Lovers). He also continues to perform with Ray Anderson’s Pocket Brass Band, Omaha Diner, and the Kamikaze Ground Crew.

Born in Berkeley, California, Bernstein moved to New York in 1978. By 1990 he had joined The Lounge Lizards, appearing on the group’s 1991 release Live in Berlin (Intuition). Shortly before that, in 1988 he formed the trio Spanish Fly with slide guitarist Dave Tronzo and tuba virtuoso Marcus Rojas. By 1995, producer Hal Willner, a fan of Spanish Fly, enlisted Bernstein as arranger for the soundtrack to Robert Altman’s film Kansas City, which led to collaborations on numerous other Willner projects, including tributes to Bill Withers, Doc Pomus, and Leonard Cohen, among many others.

In 1996, Bernstein formed Sexmob with saxophonist Briggan Krauss, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Kenny Wollesen. It remains his primary vehicle for exploring the slide trumpet, a rare instrument that he picked up in a Woodstock guitar shop back in 1977. Over two decades of recording, the group has put their singular stamp on an eclectic list of tunes by the likes of Leadbelly, John Barry, Hoagy Carmichael, Paul McCartney, Duke Ellington, Prince, Kurt Cobain, the Rolling Stones, James Brown, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, and Nino Rota. The group’s latest album, in its 20th anniversary year, is Cultural Capital, the first Sexmob recording to feature all original compositions.

From 1999 to 2008, Bernstein contributed four recordings to John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label – 1999’s Diaspora Soul (featuring members of The Lounge Lizards and Sexmob), 2002’s Diaspora Blues (featuring Sam Rivers), 2004’s Diaspora Hollywood (inspired by classic film composers and West Coast cool jazz), and 2008’s Diaspora Suite (a homecoming recorded with Bay Area musicians). Each project combined traditional cantorial songs and elements of jazz, blues, and rock.

Bernstein’s Millennial Territory Orchestra debuted with 2006’s MTO, Vol. 1, which featured large ensemble interpretations of songs by Stevie Wonder, Prince, and the Grateful Dead, as well as Benny Moten and Charlie Johnson and His Paradise Band. They followed with 2008’s We Are MTO, which included renditions of tunes by Fats Waller, Don Redman, Count Basie, and the Beatles. Their 2011 recording, MTO Plays Sly, was a tribute to the music of Sly & The Family Stone and featured the late P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell along with guest vocalists.

In 2012, Bernstein joined up with New Orleans piano master Henry Butler in the retro-flavored Butler, Bernstein and the Hot 9. Their critically acclaimed 2014 Impulse! debut, Viper’s Drag, featured spirited renditions of Fats Waller’s title track along with tunes by Jelly Roll Morton and originals by Butler. The restlessly creative Bernstein continues to juggle several working bands. During a recent residency at The Stone in NYC, he performed with Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and Universal Melody Brass Band.

Bernstein’s latest album is ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance (Royal Potato Family). In the liner notes, Bernstein mentions being enchanted by Burning Spear’s Garvey’s Ghost (Island, 1976) back in 1981, only realizing years later that it was a dub version of Marcus Garvey, Burning Spear’s Island release from the previous year. Since then, Bernstein has wanted to record an acoustic jazz trio album and have the results remade as a dub album. The first half of the release, ResoNation Trio, features Bernstein on trumpets, Scott Colley on contrabass, and Nasheet Waits on drums. To challenge himself, Bernstein eschews his main axe (slide trumpet) for this session and instead plays regular valve trumpet, G trumpet, and flugelhorn. The second half is called Ultra Resonance and features the first session tapes remixed and rearranged in dub fashion by longtime producer Scotty Hard, who also adds various keyboards, samples, and percussion to the mix. The former date is as spartan as the latter is dense, yet the two recordings (different though they are in concept and execution), are inextricably linked. I interviewed Bernstein in the summer of 2026, shortly after the release of ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance.

* * *

Troy Collins: You’ve been touring with Laurie Anderson the past few years, as documented by the recently released Let X = X (Nonesuch), which features Sexmob as Anderson’s backing band. What has it been like interpreting and rearranging her tunes for Sexmob, especially since Sexmob (in)famously doesn’t typically use pre-arranged tunes and/or setlists? And perhaps more importantly, how did this particular collaboration come about and what is working with Anderson herself like?

Steven Bernstein: Playing with Laurie has been a life-changing experience. She is completely about creation, being in the moment, acting on every inspiration, trying every idea and having fun. Her work ethic is legendary. Her ability to transform an audience is mastery. So being around her and that energy is just a powerful and positive situation. Even though a “show” is basically set once Laurie has decided on it (we are touring a completely different concert, different songs, different stories, different visuals, and a different “theme”) we/she are constantly making changes. Every show day we are at the theatre by 2:00 pm (she gets there at 11:00 am to start working with the lighting director) and we run every piece, whether a new idea comes from Laurie, me, another member of the band, a random sound that makes Laurie say “What’s that? Let’s try that in ‘___’.” Every idea is entertained and often added to the show.

The story of how this all started is beautiful. I’ve been around Laurie and known her at a distance for a long time, but the first time we really worked closely was doing Hal Willner’s Leonard Cohen show in Brighton in 2004. I arranged two songs for her, “The Guest” and “If It Be Your Will.” At Hal’s memorial she wanted to do Lou Reed’s “Gassed and Stoked.” I brought an arrangement that sounded just like the record and we played it through. She turned to me and said, “that sounds great, but I had another idea, I have this new loop” and she starts activating the loop with her violin bowing. It was a very “Laurie-style” loop: rhythmic, sonic, and not in 4/4 time. Tony and Kenny just drop in and start playing. It was grooving and effortless from the first sound. Laurie ended up testing positive for Covid and was unable to play the memorial, but a week later she calls and says how much fun she had playing with us. She said, “I’ve never had that feeling playing music” and that Warners is re-releasing her records and she was thinking of revisiting her older material (which she had never done), and asked would Sexmob play with her? You know my answer.

TC: Since you mentioned him, I’d be remiss to not ask about your years working with Hal Willner. The man’s various artist projects were significant touchstones in my development as a listener. I know he was a big fan of Spanish Fly – is that how you first met? And how did you become his go-to arranger for so many of his projects?

SB: I heard Hal’s Nino Rota record the summer of 1981 while visiting back home in Berkeley. Peter Engelhart, the legendary metal percussion maker played it for me (his daughters are some of my oldest and best friends). It changed my DNA! After that it became a thing. Who is Hal Willner? Where is Hal Willner? I did Night Music with Karen Mantler in 1989. I also played with Carla Bley, Bootsy, and Allen Toussaint on that show. Hal came up to me and said that he was a fan of Spanish Fly, that he’d been coming to our gigs at the Knitting Factory (lurking in the back I’m sure). He gave me his number and said that he would love to help us in any way he could. That led to him producing the first Spanish Fly record (on Knitting Factory records). It is a great Hal Willner production. Hal and I had very similar musical loves and ideas about music, he believed in me and kept offering me amazing opportunities. That led to a 25-year relationship. He could ask me to arrange for Elton John, Bill Frisell, Nick Cave, Lou Reed, Courtney Love, Robert Altman, Marshall Allan, U2 – it was always magic and natural. When I met him, it was pre-internet, and I would keep a pad of paper next to me during our phone conversations. His references could be Ernie Kovacs, Rahsaan, Allan Ginsberg, Martin Denny, Dorothy Parker, Anne Waldman, The Three Stooges, Gregory Corso, Fellini ... I did my best to keep up and learned a lot.

TC: Talking about Willner reminds me that you’ve done arrangements for more people than I can list, and the stylistic variety of artists is staggering. I’m curious if there’s ever been any job you feel you couldn’t or wouldn’t do?

To clarify, the beautiful thing about music is that someone else can take a song that seems unsalvageable and make something new from it that the original author may not have ever suspected was possible. Having just listened to a recent interview with Bill Frisell, I was reminded of his rendition of Madonna’s “Live To Tell,” which transforms what I would consider to be a lightweight pop song into a rhapsodic epic.

You are obviously capable of the same magic, but I wonder, have there ever been offers that you’ve refused based on the material or direction that someone wanted to go with it? Have you ever encountered a song that you felt was simply unredeemable?

SB: Well, there’s a funny story from about 8 years ago, at the beginning of Trump’s 1st term. It was a slow time (as often is the case for freelance workers) and I got an email from someone about arranging/producing some songs. The guy is a Sexmob fan, knows my work with Hal, and he has written some protest songs, tells me he thinks he can get Bono to sing on them, etc. He is not a professional musician, but this is his passion. He also has a vision of a performance piece situation, where the song is played while the listener goes down the “golden elevator” and walks somewhere else. We agree to a fee and he sends me the demo. He is playing rudimentary chords on the piano, and sings one verse, one chorus – it’s about 25 seconds. I call him and ask if there is more, he says no that’s the song. I explain that songs usually have a second or third verse, maybe a bridge, but he says no this is the song. I explain to him that it’s about 25 seconds, and if he wants it to work the way he is envisioning, (going down the elevator and walking) it needs to be at least 3 minutes long. He says, “Well do that Sexmob thing.” I talk to my wife and tell her that I don’t know if I can do this and she says “I thought you said you can make music out of anything.” So, I did and it ended up very cool!

TC: Well then, the obvious follow-up question to that is – did Bono sing on it?

SB: NO. A total pipe dream!

TC: Since we’ve been talking about arranging, I assume nothing is off limits in your own bands regarding your original tunes. Are there any pieces specifically written for say Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, or Spanish Fly that don’t translate as well from one band to the other, or do you compose your pieces so that any of your bands can perform them?

SB: Each piece is written not only for the band, but specifically for the players in each band. So, there hasn’t been much crossover. There is a piece I wrote as a commission during the pandemic that I played with Sexmob and MTO, but it really worked better as an MTO piece. But the very last phrase (the kicker) of the MTO end of night theme came from a Spanish Fly composition!

TC: Let’s move on to your new album. Your latest release for Royal Potato Family, ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance present two very different facets of your artistry – the former title finds you playing on valve trumpet and flugelhorn (instead of the ubiquitous slide trumpet) accompanied by bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, while the later features Scotty Hard remixing the trio. How did this project come about and when did you first meet and work with Scotty Hard? It seems to me your working relationship with Hard goes all the way back to the very first Sexmob album, 1998’s Din of Inequity.

SB: This project came about because of a grant from the Shifting Foundation. The idea of creating original music with the orchestration of valve trumpet, acoustic bass, and drum set has been a dream of mine for a very long time. This particular vibrational intersection is not widely used, so the unknown possibilities are vast. On a musical/improvisational/technical level it has a very specific set of challenges, and it has taken me this long to feel ready to undertake this long-held desire. Scott Colley and Nasheet were always the musicians I wanted to do this with; I have known them both a long time, and they are veteran masters of spontaneous composition. Another long-held dream has been to create a dub version of an improvisatory instrumental record. I heard Garvey’s Ghost in 1981, and it changed my DNA. Once I started making my own records, I was just waiting for the right opportunity ... and this was it. The trio record is purely conversational and in the moment; back porch music with unlimited harmonic and structural possibilities. The time spent on this record was the decades of playing and writing that preceded it. Ultra Resonance is a mirror image, in that Scott creates his pieces layer by layer, adding and subtracting sounds and rhythms – it takes weeks to build a track.

When I first started playing in The Lounge Lizards with Michael Blake on tenor, Scotty started coming to hang; he was a friend of Michael’s from Vancouver. The first session we did with him was for a Justin Warfield record on Quincy Jones’ label Qwest. It was produced by Prince Paul (I am a huge fan of De La Soul). Scotty wrote the horn chart and engineered. Scotty went on to record and produce the first four Sexmob records. I was already doing fast cuts and dropouts live, but Scotty’s mixes/arrangements shaped the sound of the band.

TC: Having just listened to Sexotica (Thirsty Ear, 2006), your collaborative effort with the production duo known as GoodandEvil (Danny Blume and Chris Castagno), I’m curious how that experience was compared to your similar efforts with Scotty Hard? How does GoodandEvil’s working method differ from Hard’s and what are your thoughts on the different outcomes?

SB: Regarding the two albums/processes – they were fundamentally different as working methods and outcomes. We went into Sexotica (which got a Grammy nomination) with the idea of creating a project that was half acoustic and half electronic. Sexmob went on and recorded all the compositions (two of them being loose jams with input from Danny Blume). Then we did a full day of overdubs with Kenny: wood percussion, metal percussion, bird whistles, and gongs. Then GoodandEvil did their magic. Some pieces skewed more acoustic, some more electronic. The idea was an even balance overall.

With Ultra Resonance Scott was given all the tracks (20 songs). The first track he made, “Titano,” was a piece that’s not on the trio record, but I felt it would be a good piece for Scotty to put his magic on. I figured he would do a “remix” of it, but he rewrote the bass line and created a brand-new piece (natch). After that it was just letting Scott experiment and follow his muse. We had mapped out a series of “zones” we wanted the pieces to be in, but everything Scotty created was totally unexpected. Part of this was the idea of intentional experimentation – on both of our parts. For me it was the idea of the acoustic record, for Scotty it was some new boxes/plug-ins that he had recently received, and the idea of not going back to his tried-and-true techniques. Also, with Sexotica I was not involved in their process, but with Scotty I would hang in the studio once the “track” was created, and was involved in arranging process (Scott claims I had 3 good ideas, I’d say more like 7.6).

As far as my thoughts on the outcomes – two singular recordings that I believe are unlike anything else in the modern recording world. I’m proud of that.

TC: Switching gears slightly (towards acoustic sounds), you’re a fan of vintage horns. I’m assuming that there are certain models you never take on tour and some that you take on the road more frequently? What are the criteria for those distinctions? And what about the slide trumpet? I’m not familiar with anyone else playing one, so where and when did you ever find one?

SB: Vintage trumpets aren’t an issue on the road. I just use the horn best suited for the music. The horn I used touring with Levon Helm was a handmade Chicago Benge from 1947. That was a horn that could project over a five-piece horn section and two electric guitars. It had amazing response and Levon could feel my beat matching his. That’s not what I need with Laurie Anderson!

Regarding the slide trumpet – I found my first horn in a guitar store in Woodstock in 1977 when I was attending Creative Music Studio. When I started Sexmob 30 years ago my old friend (and master repairman) Dick Akright in Oakland (who I met in 6th grade) built the horn I use. It’s one a kind! I’ve collected almost every brand of slide trumpet over the years, though they are not as playable as my horn.

The first horn was $25, at the time (mid-70s) and many trumpet players had one because they were cheap and easily available.

TC: Speaking of Levon Helm, what was it like working with Helm and how did that relationship come about?

SB: This is a long story. I knew Levon had been having “rent party” gigs at the barn. Tony Scherr had done some, and Erik Lawrence did as well. Levon was in danger of losing the barn, as this was a last-ditch attempt to raise some money and also make some music. Erik had invited me to play a few times, and there was a Saturday where I was available (I often did a wedding on Saturday, as I was raising a family, and those gigs paid the bills). Anyway, they mention a few songs Levon might want to do (no Band songs) and said come up early because we might rehearse. We got up there and Levon didn’t come out, so I sat with a boombox and learned a few more songs that Levon “might want to do.” It was a nice chill hang up there, and when it became clear that there was not going to be any rehearsing, I told Erik Lawrence “Don’t play what I play. You just play what you hear, and I’ll play what I hear.” That way we were both free to react to the music. We were playing with Olabelle, and Levon just walked up and got behind the drums. It was the most natural improvisation/spontaneous composition. Levon didn’t know my name, had never seen me before, just smiled at me and told me what he needed with his drum fills. It was magic, and in true Levon form, he put a song from that night on one of his CD’s. Pure improvisation – we had never met!

As far as working with him – it was some of the most magic, swinging, joyous, pure music I have ever had the opportunity to create. He taught me so much about playing in time, playing melody, playing directly from the heart to the people. He was as great and real and no bullshit and smart as you would think from his legendary status. And we had FUN. And he went from almost losing everything to winning three Grammys in eight years!

TC: Speaking of legendary performers, how did you meet pianist Henry Butler, and what was your working relationship with him like?

SB: Another long and beautiful story. In the summer of 1984, I was working with the Flying Karamazov Brothers. We spent two months doing a show at the Goodman Theater in Chicago, and then went on to do a second show at the Olympic Arts Festival in LA. When that was over, they invited me up to the Eugene Country Fair, a legendary hippie festival that was associated with Ken Kesey and the Grateful Dead family. When they asked if I’d like to join them on the Old Time New Age Chataqua tour, a traveling group of “New Vaudevillians” – musicians and environmental activists that toured small communities in the rural Northwest, camping out and putting on shows – that seemed like a better option than returning to my non-air-conditioned fifth story walk up apartment on 109th street in July.

Our first stop was our one actual “gig,” at the Vancouver Folk Festival, and we headed up there directly from the Eugene Country Fair, where we had been enjoying the kind of quality research one would associate with the Grateful Dead Community. As we entered the festival, I heard a sound I was not expecting at a folk festival – a piano player, playing and singing music that seemed like it was completely futuristic, and at the same time playing music that seemed to come from early pre-jazz America. I had never heard anything like this, and at first, I thought my ears and brain were still vibrating from my Country Fair adventures, but it was actually being played, and it was (a pre-Impulse records) Henry Butler. He completely changed my DNA and I became a fan, buying his records when they came out.

When the Kansas City soundtrack record came out on Verve records, it was a time of flowing money in the record business, CDs were selling, and I believe the Bertleman Family had bought the Verve company. In 1995 they organized a cross-country tour with the Joe Henderson Trio, Charlie Haden Quartet West, and the Kansas City All-Stars, which included many Verve artists. I was the musical director of a band that included David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron, Nicholas Payton, Christian McBride, James Carter, Mark Whitfield, etc.

I had contracted the band but was unable to find a piano player (Gerri Allen and Cyrus Chesnut had done the movie). I contacted seemingly every pianist in NYC who would fit the bill, and none were available, and I was starting to panic. I called Hal Willner to ask his advice and without missing a beat he said “did you call Henry Butler?” And that’s how it all started.

Henry and I were kindred spirits and when the tour was over he told me we would work together again. In 2011 I was doing an “MTO Plays the Early Blues” concert at a summer series in NYC. The promoter, Jay Weisman, asked if I’d like to have Henry Butler play, and I said of course, but where is he? It turned out he had an apartment in Brooklyn, post Katrina. When the concert was over Henry called me and said we should do a show with MTO playing all of his music – that was the birth of Butler Bernstein and the Hot 9 (there were 10 people in the band). As far as my working relationship, he totally trusted my bandleading instincts and arranging, and I was always awed and inspired by the music flowing out of him.

TC: You bring up a salient point. Around the time of the Kansas City soundtrack, there seemed to be a very healthy major label interest in jazz that benefitted musicians of all stripes, even those somewhat on the fringe (James Carter, Don Byron, David Murray, etc.), which to me, evoked the pre-Young Lions era, when major labels signed post-loft jazz artists like Anthony Braxton, Arthur Blythe, and Henry Threadgill.

Much has changed since then. I’m curious what your thoughts are on that phenomenon? How have you adapted to the changing fortunes of the recording business? And what do you foresee for the future?

SB: Well, the beautiful thing is that I have been DIY since the beginning. I think the budget of the first Spanish Fly record (which was on Knitting Factory Records) was 3K, and Hal Willner produced it! I personally have never really had a record contract where I was signed and had a budget. I’ve had a few independent contracts, and records funded by public and private grants. That is the way everything is now, so it’s just the way I’ve always been able to create new things. And that’s what it’s about, creating new things.

TC: In reference to creating new things, I’m curious about your thoughts on live performance versus studio recording. Studio recordings of Sexmob often feature a fair amount of electronic manipulation and remixing, much like Ultra Resonance. What are your thoughts on the difference between purely acoustic performances versus such heavily processed and studio manipulated recordings? Do you vary your approach towards playing depending on the situation?

SB: My feeling is that once Electric Ladyland and The White Album came out, there was no turning back. Even my albums that aren’t “heavily electronically processed” (aka produced by Scotty Hard) feature mixes that are very specific, often times emphasizing certain frequencies, the same way a painter will use certain colors to draw the eye. I believe a record should be a mind-altering listening experience. ResoNation Trio is also a studio record, although one that creates a vision of an imagined acoustic experience. As far as playing, I just do the best I can when the recording light is on!

TC: Let’s go back to those early, heady days. According to your bio, you grew up in the Berkeley area and were friends with Peter Apfelbaum, with whom you regularly attended jazz gigs. There was mention of an “eye-opening gig” by the Art Ensemble of Chicago at San Francisco’s Great American Music Hall. What was it about that particular show that resonated with you?

SB: It was just seeing them live after listening to the records for two years. The magic and visceral-ness of it. There is magic that happens when you are in the room, seeing the musicians and feeling the vibrations, sharing the communion of music. We also met them that night. We were pretty heady. We went to their dressing room and banged out “Nfamoudou-Boudougou” on the door. They were certainly shocked to open the door and see two scruffy teenagers.

They welcomed Peter and me into the dressing room, and that started a relationship that continues to this day (Peter is still in touch with Roscoe). When I moved to NYC I went to see the AEC at the Public Theatre, either late 1979 or early 1980. Now when we went to shows in the Bay Area everyone was dressed hippie funky, so that’s how I showed up, probably in overalls and a t-shirt. I go backstage after the show and am totally self-conscious to be surrounded by well-dressed urban New Yorkers in Kente Cloth and immaculate jewelry. Lester opens up the dressing room door, peeks out at all the “beautiful people” and says “BERNSTEIN get in here!” closes the door, points to the table and says “you can roll a joint, right?” (I could).

TC: Now that’s funny. I certainly remember my one and only time seeing the Art Ensemble of Chicago. It was in Philadelphia, at The Clef Club. Jarman wasn’t touring with them at this point, but it was still magical, ceremonial even.

One group I regretfully never saw was The Lounge Lizards. You were a member of The Lounge Lizards in the 1990s. How did that association come about? And while bandleader John Lurie has had an unusual (to say the least) life and career path since then, I was wondering, do you still have any contact with him?

SB: I have yet another tall tale to tell. It was summer of 1989 and I was touring with Chautauqua again, the same group of people I was touring with when I first heard Henry Butler in 1984. Back then we had answering machines that you called into and used a beeper to retrieve your messages (This is pre cell phones). I was in a small town somewhere, probably Idaho or Montana, and I went to a payphone and checked my messages, and I heard a message from John’s assistant saying to call John up because he was interested in having me join The Lounge Lizards. Needless to say I was beyond excited, because The Lounge Lizards was the “Premiere Band” on the downtown scene.

I call John up and the first thing he says to me is “Do you have a suit?” The next thing he says to me is “you’re not gonna get a lot of solos.” Luckily, the tour was heading to a place of general civilization (Port Townsend) and I was able to put together a tape so John had an idea of what my playing was like, and that September I started rehearsing with the band.

I still talk with John. The most recent project we did together was working on music for his film, that was two summers ago. We did music for Painting with John, and there was an excellent and entertaining episode in season three (I believe) that featured the making of the soundtrack, which really showed the process that we use.

Early on with The Lounge Lizards I started to arrange and transcribe for John, first working on Fishing with John, which led to arranging and conducting soundtracks such as Get Shorty and Excess Baggage. Get Shorty was the summer of 1995, and John and I would spend 12 hours a day together as I transcribed his ideas and put them into notated forms.

TC: I’m glad to hear you’re still in contact with John. Speaking of the 1990s, you recorded four albums in the late 1990s to early 2000s for John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label: Diaspora Soul (1999); Diaspora Blues (2002); Diaspora Hollywood (2004); and Diaspora Suite (2008). As a fan of those albums, I’m curious if you ever return to any of those tunes or arrangements?

SB: I’m glad you brought up those records. I love the Diaspora series too. Yes, it lives on. I wrote big band arrangements of some of this music for Arturo O’Farril and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra for two different concerts. I arranged a version of “Ani Mamin,” which I recorded with saxophones and valve trumpet on Diaspora Soul, reimagined as a tribute to Eddie Palmer and Conjunto Libre, arranged now for four trombones and slide trumpet. I learned that Barry Rogers, the architect of the New York salsa trombone sound, was raised in Brooklyn and his father and uncle sang with Moshe Kousevvitskey’s choir. Full circle New York history for you. I also recorded a version of “Cha” with Arturo and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra. We recorded it during the pandemic, so it's all over-dubbed. “Cha” was inspired by John Zorn’s composing for Masada, and I created an arrangement inspired by Machito. I recently revisited the Diaspora Blues music alongside Arturo O’Farrill, Anat Cohen, and a small version of the Afro Latin Jazz Ensemble. This October at the Stone I'll be premiering a duo version of the Diaspora music with Arturo O’Farrill, so the music lives on, and keeps evolving.

TC: What other musical projects or performances do you have coming up in the near future?

SB: Here are a few upcoming shows:

September 23-29: Laurie Anderson and Sexmob, West Coast Tour and Chicago October 1: Helm Family Ramble in Brooklyn October 2: ResoNation Trio at Tempo, Kingston NY October 28: ResoNation Trio at The Stone October 29: Ultra Resonance at The Stone October 30: Diaspora Special Edition with Arturo O’Farrill at The Stone October 31: Sexmob Kurt Weill Halloween at The Stone

Sexmob Live at Carambolage, Bolzano (the last night of our March 2026 European tour) will be released at the end of the year. It’s our first documentation of the “new sound” of the band with Kenny’s electro drums in the mix.

And more upcoming projects that I’m not quite ready to announce.

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.album: The Sound of the Abbey
items.excerpt:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhyt
items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了十三支比利时创新乐团在帕克修道院录制的作品，以器乐为主，融合比利时民间音乐与世界音乐传统。专辑跨越多种风格：罗姆人小提琴、迪加莱摇摆乐、地中海阿拉伯风格ud弹唱、巴洛克风格的曼陀林与古钢琴合奏、亚美尼亚杜瓦管独奏、凯尔特喉音配爵士鼓组与匈牙利古琴等。风琴作为核心乐器贯穿始终，部分作品带有即兴色彩。制作耗时三年，利用古老石建筑的天然混响营造温暖声场，赋予专辑统一的精神气质。整体虽风格多元却具有内在连贯性，音乐既出人意料又兼具安抚感，展现了修道院空间对创作灵感的深层影响。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦俄罗斯占领区约两万乌克兰儿童被强制带离父母的战争罪行，以传统与原创曲目交织呈现沉重的社会议题。乌克兰裔加拿大人Marichka分别在两国召集两组音乐家，以弓弦乐器、班杜拉琴和钢琴为主要编制，其中包含一位曾是被掳儿童后归来的16岁演奏者。歌词取材于乌克兰古老的送女外出务工民歌，传统上象征离散之痛，如今直接映射当代被偷走的儿童命运。音乐风格在温柔低吟与激进粗粝之间切换，rusalka（斯拉夫传说中的自然精灵）意象贯穿其中，赋予作品神话与仪式色彩。专辑将传统民谣置于现代战争语境之下，演奏与歌词形成强烈张力，是世界音乐领域中具有明确政治立场与文化深度的作品。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了上世纪七十至八十年代圣多美和普林西比群岛的Puxa音乐，是继第一卷之后的续作。Puxa是一种融合多种非洲葡萄牙语殖民地节奏的复杂音乐形态，吸纳了merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等元素，据说配合舞蹈可召唤或驱赶灵体。这种音乐风格在葡萄牙殖民时期曾遭禁，却顽强延续下来。专辑收录超过十五首曲目，展现多层吉他交织、复调式人声对话的特点，乐手们在失重的律动中即兴铺展，呈现出能够持续数小时的现场能量。从Pedro Lima的炽热乐队到Sangazuza的简约律动，再到Africa Negra的政治宣言曲目，每首作品都展示了岛屿特有的音乐语言与舞蹈传统的紧密结合。
