items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴音乐厅完成了一场两小时的不插电独奏即兴录音，后期混入人声采样、打击乐、循环段落、田野录音与拾得音效，形成一张介于即兴爵士、世界音乐与声音实验之间的作品。Sosa 拒绝风格归类，强调首遍即录的直觉性，以'少即是多'为创作信条，在空旷音乐厅的声学共鸣中延展钢琴的泛音与触感。专辑创作背景与疫情封锁、个人生活转折交织，Sosa 认为音乐应超越市场分类与算法逻辑，回归人类精神共鸣与文化传统的双重根基。整体呈现一种冥想式、不急于抵达的钢琴即兴美学，适合对跨文化即兴与声音探索感兴趣的听众。

items._genre: acousmatic / electroacoustic / sound art / field recording
items._cn_summary: 本乐评介绍了两部声音艺术作品的合辑。Andrew Czink的《Iron Emerald》探讨声音之间的关系如何暗示其可辨识声源之外的意义，属于典型的声学音乐（acousmatic music）创作思路。Zazie Productions的《Spectral Ode to Synesthesia》则利用脉冲噪声、拾得物品、田野录音等素材构建空间化的声音作品，带有明确的通感体验意图。两部作品都偏向实验性聆听，强调声音的物质性与空间感，而非传统旋律或节奏结构。该乐评内容较为简短，提供了作品的创作手法和概念框架，但缺少对实际听觉效果的深入描述。作为一场声音艺术展演的记录，文章对了解当代声学音乐创作方向有一定参考价值，但信息深度有限。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the most unique and stranger acts to emerge from the 70s prog scene was bizarre in many waysactually. AKASHA emerged from Norway, a nation currently prolific to progressive music in the 21stcentury wasn't a major player in the golden years of prog rock. And this band didn't come from Oslo,This short-lived act came from one of the most northern regions of all of Europe and formed in thesmall Arctic fishing village of Kj�llefjord. But what makes this band strange is that it reallydidn't sound like any other act of the day despite smatterings of influences piled into the schizoidrandom musical styles that seemed to find bits and pieces derived from Genesis, Pink Floyd, TheMoody Blues and King Crimson amongst others. The band was a quintet featuring Sverre Svendsen onlead vocals and mellotrons, Jens Ivar Andreassen on guitars, Mellotron, synthesizers, piano, organ,Arild Andreassen on bass, Kjell Evensen on drums and also included are the lyrics and poetry of Tor-Jony Hansen. AKASHA released only one mere album in 1977 and given its extreme remote location with littleopportunity for promotion or touring for that matter, the album has become one of those extremerarities. The strange artifact is also unique in that it displays the track listings on the frontcover but what really sets this one apart is the mishmash of music sounds that include hypnoticspace rock, freaky sound generated through synthesizers and mellotrons and a schizophrenic hairpinpropensity to simply morph into other music styles midstream reminding me a bit of the GermanKrautrock act Silberbart albeit with less guitar bombast. Likewise the band recorded in a bomb-proofcellar which was used as a shelter in the basement of a hotel in the small town of Finnsnes, Norwaywhich gives the production an interesting uniqueness much in the way of the band German Oak whichrecorded in a similar bomb shelter.The lengthy "Isle Of Kawi" begins the epic journey sounding something like the French Archaĩa withrapid fire synthesized arpeggios and what sounds like some sort of folk music but then sort ofshifts gears and sounds a bit more like something Pulsar would've conjured up on the first tworeleases. With this opening track it feels like you've stumbled into some lost classic musical treatas the sonic display is brooding and dark and on par with early Univers Zero for apocalyptic motifsof complete detachment from established paradigms. The track continues to morph into a labyrinthinedisplay of interesting twists and turns. The album quickly reveals its greatest flaw though on thesecond track "Bondage" which finds the lackluster vocal style of Sverre Svendsen who delivers arather mopey scatter-brained performance over some sort of drugged out lounge music before the trackbursts into rapid-fire key arpeggios that prognosticate the work of Philip Glass on "Glassworks" andhis classic "Koyaanisqatsi." And then off to some early "Trespass" styled Genesis sounding prog!The instrumental combo effect of "Recitativ" and "Electronic Nightmare" displays the band at itsmost unhinged with the first track in full rock mode for the first time only with strange guitarriffs and off-kilter contrapuntal elements. Unlike the prior tracks, this one has pounding drums anda guitar solo. The second on the other hand goes into outer space and features avant-gardeexperimentalism carried out through overlayering electronic effects sounding more Tangerine Dream orKlaus Schulze with a steady rhythmic pulse of Jean Michel Jarre. "Death Hymn" combines faster rockwith the electronics and then breaks into some sort of rockin' the classics keyboard freneticismmore in vein of The Nice. But wait! There's more - it then morphs into a slow oozing space rockmotif with detached spoken word lyrics which are in English. "Light And Darkness" is one of the mostschizoid tracks with several changes of tempos, styles and rich in off-kilter time signatures andjust plain bonkers ideas. More steeped in rock but drenched in mellotrons and atmospheric weirdnessas well."The Trip" offers the most normal track on board and actually sticks to a bluesy rock format formost of its run however the closing "Man And The Void" however returns to the restless nature of thealbum with a space rock intro that quickly shifts into strange guitar chord riffs and at timesreminds me of Gnidrolog but less structured and more freeform in many ways. This album offers thetrue spirit of DIY musical ambitions overcoming the extreme remote geography, lack of recordingfacilities and production extravaganzas. This band truly did things its own way on its own terms.Despite the imperfections of weak vocals, lackluster production and blatant disregard for any sortof unified sound, this album will appeal to those seeking out the most unapologetically originalalbums of the era and despite the flaws more than makes up for in its sheer creative audacity thatmakes AKASHA really a difficult band to classify with its symphonic prog, Krautrock and eclecticmusic spirit. For my tastes this one is quite appealing.

items._cn_summary: 这张1977年挪威专辑来自北极圈内的偏远渔村，由五位乐手在小镇酒店的防空洞中录制完成，录音环境的特殊性赋予了作品独特的声学质感。乐队将Genesis的诗意、Pink Floyd的空灵、Krautrock的机械律动与King Crimson的黑暗气质熔于一炉，频繁在曲中段切换风格，呈现出碎片化但充满探索精神的结构。Mellotron与合成器的大量运用营造出催眠般的太空氛围，长篇器乐段落尤其展现出实验倾向。然而主唱的演绎被乐评批评为缺乏感染力，成为专辑的明显短板。整体而言，这是一张融合多种前卫元素、带有强烈个人印记的稀有作品，适合对早期实验性前卫摇滚感兴趣的听众。

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Following the iconic 2001 album "Blackwater Park", Opeth had planned to release a double album. However, encouraged by Jonas Renkse (Katatonia), the Swedish band led by Mikael ��kerfeldt decided to release two albums simultaneously, each with a distinct musical approach: "Damnation," more progressive and less aggressive -whose release was delayed once it was completed due to a commercial decision by the record label- and "Deliverance" (2002), which is likely one of the band's heaviest, darkest, and most murky albums.Low tunings, thick distortion, persistent riffs, Martin Lopez's dizzying and at times excessive double-bass drumming, and ��kerfeldt's hellish guttural displays give the album its monolithic and brutal character, in tracks like the frenetic "Wreath" with its corrosive death metal sounds, the eponymous and superb "Deliverance," with its galloping and versatile riffs, hypnotic and hazy acoustic interludes, and a devastating instrumental finale led by guitarist Peter Lindgren, or the gothic darkness of "Master's Apprentices," featuring Steven Wilson's distinctive touch as he accompanies �kerfeldt with his melancholic voice and guitars.An atmosphere of extreme hostility from which "Deliverance" momentarily departs with "A Fair Judgment," which delves into the intricacies of progressive metal and evokes Floydian and Crimsonian influences in its structure, thickening in its final third with Lindgren's forceful, Black Sabbath-esque riffs -probably the best track on the album- and with the stripped-down "For Absent Friends," a brief and refreshing electro-acoustic tribute to the Genesis song of the same name, which offers a breather before the album plunges back into its darker textures.The experimental "By the Pain I See in Others" takes Opeth's progressive death metal into more twisted and dissonant territory, guided by �kerfeldt's cavernous and unsettling vocals to an intimidating new level and featuring a disconcerting circus-like middle section that evokes the grotesque theater of German composer Kurt Weill. After its musical development fades away, the track leaves a prolonged silence, interrupted by backward-played vocals from fragments of "Master's Apprentices," bringing the great album "Deliverance" to a close with a suspended, spectral echo.4 stars

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了乐队与Steven Wilson合作的成功路线，将前卫摇滚的复杂结构注入极端金属框架。低音调弦搭配密集双踩鼓点构成沉重基调，而Åkerfeldt的咆哮人声与阴郁的吉他即兴段落形成张力。专辑中段穿插了带有Pink Floyd与King Crimson影子的渐进段落，以及向Genesis致敬的短篇原声作品，在金属压迫感中提供了呼吸空间。终曲引入倒放人声与剧场化中段，实验性元素隐现其中。整体虽以金属为核心，但其在结构拓展与氛围营造上的手法使其超出常规死亡金属范畴，与暗潮与前卫摇滚听众的审美亦有交集。

items.body: Review by Beautiful Scarlet — An excellent work of Jazz Fusion. The synths, fretless bass, electric guitar, and piano all mesh together very well. Normally, I would like to assess each track; however, with an album like this, I find it difficult. There is a very strong sense of cohesion in "Dr. Aftershave." The songs blend very well, encouraging me to let the album play through in its entirety every time I go to listen. And while I also appreciate Missus Beastly' second and fourth albums, I think this one, "Dr. Aftershave," is the most consistent. As an album, it is the best. In my opinion, it does not have weaker tracks that I'd like to skip.

items._cn_summary: 这张1976年的专辑展现了融合爵士的成熟面貌，以无品贝斯、电吉他、合成器与钢琴为核心乐器编织出紧密交织的声响纹理。整张作品呈现出高度的内部统一性，曲目之间自然过渡，毫无断裂感，乐评人评价其没有任何需要跳过的弱轨，这种一致性正是融合爵士美学中较少被强调的特质。Missus Beastly作为德国乐队，其作品在融合爵士框架中融入了欧陆即兴传统的元素，与美式fusion的炫技路线有所不同，键盘与吉他的对话更倾向于氛围与结构的探索。贝斯线条的无品处理为低音区提供了独特的滑动质感，合成器的使用并非为了制造太空感或未来感，而是作为音色织体的补充层，与原声乐器形成有机融合。

items.body: In the 1980s, Belgium was practically the home of underground Electro. Bands such as Front 242, The Neon Judgement, The Klinik, A Split Second, SA42, àGrumh, The Weathermen ao were among the biggest names of the scene, and their influence can still be heard in artists today. One group that emerged in the late 1980s, and remains in my opinion unfairly overlooked, is Philadelphia Five. Mark Borgions and Jo Lijnen debuted with the maxi-singles “Bump! Jerry” and “Heaven,” followed by the album “Trilogy” in 1990. Their sound stood apart from that of many of the aforementioned bands. It was underground and thoroughly Electro, but perhaps less cold and austere, with even a touch of humor – or perhaps self-deprecation. Their cover of Boney M is a perfect example of this, and something quite unheard of at the time. Sadly, the duo eventually disappeared from the scene, partly because of the terrible treatment they received from their record label, KK Records. At the time, the Belgian label was synonymous with quality, and the older generation among us will remember artists such as Vomito Negro, Cat Rapes Dog, Insekt, The Force Dimension, Lassigue Bendthaus, and many others. Unfortunately, however, it would later become clear that the label did not always pay its artists. For Philadelphia Five, this marked the end of the road. And yet, more than 30 years later, Philadelphia Five has clearly not been forgotten. Last year, for instance, Philadelphia Five performed at the notorious Ombra Festival in Barcelona, while this year they are scheduled to appear at Belgium’s BIM Festival. For years, I had wondered what had become of Philadelphia Five. So when one of our loyal readers – who will probably recognize themselves here – suggested that I get in touch with the band, I took the opportunity. I eventually managed to convince Mark and Jo to sit down with me for a retrospective interview. What followed is a fascinating conversation that looks back at the band’s history while also opening a window onto today’s Electro and underground scene. This interview is a tribute, but above all, it is an expression of gratitude for the music these two artists created all those years ago. Their story follows below. (Picture credits by Remo Perrotti / Interview courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Philadelphia Five interview Q: The Philadelphia Five music immediately takes us back more than 35 years. What was your musical background at the time? Who were your main influences, role models, or even muses? And how did Philadelphia Five actually come into being, which I believe was briefly a trio in the beginning, if I remember correctly? Jo: My roots go way back. I remember Woodstock being my first musical revelation, over a love/hate relationship with Disco, to Punk. The first records I ever bought, I bought in London in the late ’70s were Jimi Hendrix, Tuxedomoon, Rory Gallagher, Sex Pistols. The Great Rick’n Roll Swindle completely blew my mind. I was in university with Mark’s sister, and it’s through her we met midsummer 1982. I had a collective / band called Das V.E.R. with some friends, organizing events and playing gigs with covers of Joy Division, Cabaret Voltaire and the likes. I played a Yamaha CS15. Mark: I was about 15 then and I thought that extremely cool. I myself had a fondness for the early Electronic New-Wave / Post-Punk scene and all things with a good four-to-the-floor / bass / arpeggio combination. I was into buying records and regularly got invited to DJ on their events, private and public. I only played Electro, which made some people’s head explode back then. But I was completely fascinated by the music. Through a friend, my dad had good pricing deals on Roland gear, and I got an SH-101 and a TR-808 when they were still in production. So, we both had a fondness for synths, and one thing led to another. First time we played a set together was at a private party. We called ourselves De Apostels Van De Auto-Erotische Stoet and I remember we played covers of A Blaze Colour’s “The New Ones”, “Warm Leatherette” (of course), Mistral’s “Jamie” and a couple of original songs.  Jo: Not long after that, we changed our name to Philadelphia Five. We remained a duo until 1987, when Ilse Stalmans joined the band. That coincided with our first interview – with the tape magazine Mad in Belgium. So she is part of that. We had fun with other musicians, too. But quite soon, both for practical and musical reasons, we returned to being a duo. Mark: The issue of MiB included our version of Boney M’s “Baby Do You Wanna Bump”, recorded on a 4-track Tascam. Enter Jo Verbruggen. He had a record store in Sint Niklaas and was about to launch a record label. He heard our track and showed an interest in signing us. And so we got signed to KK Records before it really existed and headed to Tienen, to Luc Van Acker’s studio to record our first vinyl. Q: I find the period in which Philadelphia Five emerged extremely interesting, because in the late ’80s there seemed to be a kind of cross-pollination between the underground Electro scene on the one hand and the rise of New-Beat on the other. How did you experience that musical crossroads, and what impact did it have on your own music? Jo: In the early 80’s there was a new wave of bands using new electronic instruments. Gary Numan (“Living Ornaments”), Heaven 17 (“Penthouse” and “Pavement”), Laurie Anderson (“Big Science”) come to mind. All that had led me to buy that CS15, but also a programmable AV computer and a Philips Videomixer. There was all sorts of interesting new technology. Mark: When I started buying records, it was the time of the early Some Bizzare and Mute releases. I was really very much into that sort of thing. The early Human League albums, Kraftwerk, The New Romantics scene. Some of that music started appearing on hit lists. The sound of the drums, the heavy presence of synths, it all appealed to me very much. That and some more Experimental and underground bands like Throbbing Gristle. That was the music that formed me. New-Beat started happening when we had found our thing already. I remember Jo from  KK Records sent us to Stonesound Studios in The Netherlands, because they had recorded “The Sound Of C”, and Jo really wanted “Heaven” to sound like that. But it was never really what we wanted. And we clashed with the engineer quite a few times over sound vs production quality issues. In hindsight, I think “Heaven” and “Trilogy” sound too clean.  It was because of New-Beat that KK Records wanted stuff like “Bonga Walk” on “Heaven”, and I think we may have pushed that track somewhat more in the New-Beat direction than we should have. I was never a fan of that scene. It all felt too clean, too commercial. There were more than enough interesting sounds out there to keep myself busy.  Jo: Still, we kept our eye on what was going on with New-Beat. We visited the New-Beat temples to see what was happening. “Bonga Walk”, in essence based on an Italian head banging tradition, just happened to fit the mold. But I don’t remember it being played much in those clubs. It’s only years later that the song appeared on that definite New-Beat compilation. Mark: We did get to do some gigs because of New-Beat’s popularity, I’m sure. And we more than once had issues with the venues because we wanted to play live as much as we could, when most acts were just dancers and a playback tape. It’s because of New-Beat that we played in places like Ancienne Belgique (the Antwerp club, not the Brussels venue). That would not have happened otherwise, I’m quite sure.  Q: One thing I always found quite original about the Philadelphia Five songs was that they sounded less cold and dark than many Belgian EBM groups of that time. To me, you sounded more accessible and harder to pigeonhole into a specific genre. Was this a conscious choice, or because of what you just told? And what was your relationship like with other Belgian bands from that era? Mark: I think it just comes from all we just laid out. I think we didn’t take it all too seriously, and we had fun toying around with the machinery. Not being real musicians. We had lyrics that were not so serious, sometimes just read from stupid books, manuals or magazines.  Jo: Ho there! Those songs definitely had an autobiographical undertone! Songs like “Jerry”, “I Am Shared” and “Watch Out” were straight from the soul. Also, a lot of the stuff that never made it to vinyl was very personal. Mark: We liked the dance aspect of it more than the doom part. And we both don’t have graveyard voices. That also. I don’t think we ever really were part of the Belgian scene, in so much as that was a thing. We did meet some bands through KK Records and concerts, but we were mostly just busy with our own things. Jo: Our manager, Dries Vandermeersch (aka MDM-management), did help us a lot in connecting with the right people. He arranged for us to play in Germany and The Netherlands. And he connected us to Jo Casters and Duc Nhan Nguyen, who both did FOH for a couple of our shows.  Q: What made you completely different was the rather surprising – and perhaps somewhat daring – cover of “Baby Do You Wanna Bump” by Boney M. The crazy thing is that it worked perfectly and really caught on. What on earth had you used or drunk back then to come up with such an idea (lol)? And more seriously: how did that version come together, and do you know if anyone from the Boney M camp ever heard it? Mark: The cover was a direct result of us really liking the directness of the original. There was very little cross-genre consideration, really. The bassline just carries the song in the same way we had basslines pushing our songs forward. The bass is very much like a plucky sequencer sequence, what’s not to like? Jo: I remember when I started going out as a teenager, dancing to “Bump” had a puberal intimacy thing going, too. And musically, I always felt it stood above most of the commercial Disco tunes. We know that Frank Farian was surprised and flattered by our cover request. He had made the song in ’74 in his home studio. Boney M was the packaging for tv appearances. Mark: I’m not sure if he ever heard ours, though. He never told us. I know he received his share of the rights, though. Q: I have to admit that Boney M has always been one of my ‘guilty pleasures’, largely because of those deep, fat bass lines. How about you guys – what was the attraction for you? Mark: So the way I remember it, when I was a young kid, you had ABBA folk and Boney M Folk. I definitely was BONEY M. Yes, I too liked the beats and the dominant bass lines. Stuff like Amii Stewart’s “Knock On Wood” or Georgio Moroder’s “From Here To Eternity” (which we covered  also), Divine and later even some Stock Aitken & Waterman all had the same influence on us. Not all of that was synth stuff, and it wasn’t underground. But it had the same structure and that’s why we liked it. Repetitive sequences, and a hard hitting percussive elements too.  Q: The Philadelphia Five album “Trilogy” (1990) was released on KK Records. In hindsight, some artists have suggested that KK Records was not exactly known for paying royalties properly, which raises questions about how bands were treated. What were your own experiences? Mark: Royalty issues, really?!? (LOL). We got to know Jo from day one of his label venture. “Bump! Jerry” was catalog Kk002, but as I remember it was the first KK release to come out. Jo was always overly enthusiastic. But the royalty statements were  sketchy. It was Maurice Engelen (who lived in the same town I lived) who told me about what was going on in The States. One day he called me up:’“you do know you’ve got a big dancefloor hit in the States, right?’ We knew nothing about that. ‘Why didn’t you come to us with your music?’ Us being Antler/Subway. I guess because he never asked? Later, when discogs came to be, we learned about compilations and foreign pressings we never knew about back then. Q: KK Records was certainly a label many people looked up to because of the big names on its roster. Was there a real sense of connection between those bands, and does something like that truly exist in a music scene? Jo: In the pre-digital years, there was no real contact between the KK bands, or other bands from the scene. But around 2020 that changed for me. I started having online conversations with people from Vomito Negro, Force Dimensions, Kode Iv, Blue Eyed Christ, Insekt, … We all had one thing in common: decades of KK issues. There even was talk about collective legal initiatives, but those never happened for various reasons. We ourselves managed to formally regain our rights in 2019, after they were wrongfully included in the KK catalog transfer from Coble to Warner. Luckily, we had signed contracts that returned the rights to us after “Trilogy”. So after some back and forth, Warner returned them, on the condition we would not retroactively start discussing wrongfully collected rights of all compilation releases to that date. All that happened in good faith and we are glad we have everything back in our hands. Q: Philadelphia Five was certainly not a one-hit wonder, but after “Trilogy” nothing else followed. Was that partly due to the KK Records experience, or were there other reasons? And did you record songs back then that were never released? Mark: The KK experience had a lot to do with it. Mainly in a sense that Jo wanted us to produce more ‘hit’ stuff and became pushy about that. To be honest, from our end, “Trilogy” was set up as our way to end the KK contract. Somewhere in the liner notes it says something about never ever playing that music again. We meant it. I personally was empty and unhappy about release pressure. The joy was gone. Our last show in Germany didn’t go too well and when we came home, I deleted a lot of the music we had on the W30, which was our main workstation. All “Not Leaving Without Jerry samples” are gone. Other stuff too. Now, after close to 40 years, I hope it’s OK to revise that Never statement.  Q: Looking back today, how do you feel about the album “Trilogy”, and what memories have stayed with you from the entire production process? Mark: To us, what came before “Trilogy” is more important. The individual releases of “Bump! Jerry” and “Heaven” are closer to our hearts. I like that there’s a remix thing going on with the tracks, but today I like the originals more. The way we recorded a lot of the music was 24 tracks of loops, sequences and other repetitions, and then we sort of ‘played’ the master mix on the console. So every time we played a song to a stereo end mix, it was somewhat differently constructed. I also remember making edits on a physical cut table. Lots of tape scrubbing. Some of it is in the final mixes.  Jo: When we were in Luc Van Acker’s then new studio to record “Bump! Jerry”, it was all about the feel and the sound. The recording had a bit of a lo-fi thing going. When we did the remix of “Bump” and “Jerry” at Stonesound, the engineer there did nothing but complain about the lo-fi quality of the recording. But it had all the feel we wanted, and that was the most important thing. Some of that feel got lost on the “Trilogy” versions.  Q: One thing I always remember from several songs were the explicit moans and suggestive – not to say sexually charged – samples. “Heaven” is just one example. Was that simply youthful provocation, or was there something more behind it? And what inspired you lyrically in general? Mark: We were two young guys in early video store days. No wonder we heard a lot of silly and suggestive dialogue and moaning (LOL). Although the “Heaven” samples are from a documentary by Diane Keaton. Not from cheesy porn. But some of the moaning is! Some came from a cassette tape we bought on a trip to Italy, at a gas station. The tape has seashore sounds on one side of the stereo, moaning on the other. And Italian dirty talk of which we understood nothing on the B side. Still have that tape somewhere. We were just looking for good material to sample. Maurice Engelen once told me he was envious of our samples. As it turns out, so much so that he later named one of his own releases “Heaven Is An Orgasm”. You’re welcome, Maurice.  Q: Your music comes from an era when Electro was still largely made with analog equipment – a very different world from today. What did your home studio look like back then? And how do you view that period in relation to today’s digital production, software synths, AI in music, and all the technological evolutions that have taken place? Have you kept up with these developments yourselves? Mark: Our first gear was pre-MIDI. The CS15, SH-101 and MC-202 were CV/Gate, and there was din sync to the TR-808. The Juno-60 had its own protocol. Later we bought a second 808, a Moog Prodigy, and two Roland samplers, an S-50 and the W-30. Those each had their own sort of sequencer. And they had MIDI. We had a Roland sync box that hooked the MIDI to DIN and could lay a click track. At home we recorded on a PortaOne. Later I bought a second hand Yamaha TG77, which I was told came from Daniel B. But we never used that on a recording. Mostly, we used samples of the old gear on the samplers.  Jo: We also had Dynacord drum pads and modules, one of which could hold very short samples. The bass drum module is on all the old recordings and has a very specific sound. Mark: I’ve remained a gear head. I toyed around with early Propellerheads stuff and later landed on Ableton Live, which I still use today. I had a time when I was exploring soft synths, but I really missed the immediacy of knob fiddling. Live was the first software that communicated with the old analog gear in ways that were actually working. I’ve always added gear. I’ve got a decent modular setup that keeps growing and I have finally learned to program the TG77. Most stuff I do now still comes mainly out of the analog gear, but the sequencing is so much easier in Ableton. Now, all is connected to Live for sequencing, recording, scene organizing and mixing. I like the workflow. As for AI, I have mixed feelings. I use mastering plugins that rely on it and that’s wonderful. But it will never replace the heart of the music, I think. I hope. And AI generated crap is truly problematic. I want to stay away from that as far as I can. If nothing else, it stimulates me to push things the other way as much as possible.  Q: How did Philadelphia Five actually come to an end, and what happened afterwards? Did you stay in touch, continue making music individually, or remain connected to one scene or another? Mark: At some moment in time, we had lost the joy. The thing we started for in the first place. We kept in contact. Not always as active, but we never lost sight of each other. I kept playing with the gear. But never really results oriented.  Jo: The financial shenanigans with KK drained a lot of our energy. And the joy. But also: we had both started our ‘grown up life’, which took most of our focus. So it ended a natural end. But every now and then, we had ad hoc creative encounters. Q: I believe Mark remained active in the broader artistic world, but what about you, Jo? What artistic paths did you follow afterwards? And more broadly, what do Art and creation mean to you personally? Jo: In the late 80’s, I started zaal BELGIE in Hasselt, which ran on a bunch of passionate volunteers. BELGIE quickly grew in scope – artistically and infrastructural. That became Kunstencentrum BELGIE vzw, a multidisciplinary art center with a wide scope of international productions and activity. A lot of very interesting artists performed there, some even had residencies. Last March, I retired, but I stay very involved. Q: At that time, Belgium was on the world map as a pioneering land of Electronic music – it all felt new, visionary, and focused on the future. Contemporary Electro, on the other hand, often seems to look back, especially to the ’80s. How do you see that? Do you think today’s artists are less innovative, or is that perhaps too simplistic? Mark: Oh but I think there’s plenty of interesting music out there. I think it’s mainly that the market has changed. It sometimes feels like there’s no longer such a thing as the underground or the alternative. It’s all equal to a certain extend. Look at festivals like Dour, there’s all these acts I’ve never heard of, yet they play the big stages and it’s completely sold out. That would not have happened in our days. And with today’s digital distribution, even the smallest release is global. But there’s also an over-saturation. And it’s a different process to find the interesting music. Maybe the last true technical innovation came with the accessibility of synths, and how our generation f*cked around with that new technology, not knowing anything about music theory. And with that, I think it’s inevitable that there’s people harvesting what people in the 80’s sowed. And I think it’s quite flattering that artists I enjoy now, take time to let me know that our music did something in their musical education. But as I just said, I think there’s plenty of music that walks interesting paths, still today.  Jo: Yet it’s true, a lot of what is happening now feels less impulsive. Everything is more constructed by marketing and economics. Innovation is a buzz word, but it’s different from how we did it in the 80’s and 90’s. Back then, it was all DIY. New things came from the base and worked themselves up from there. Coloring outside the lines was adventurous, not only in music. Q: Last year Philadelphia Five were invited to play at the big OmbraFestival in Barcelona, and at the end of this year you’ll be playing in Belgium at the legendary BIM Fest. Has Philadelphia Five been given a second life? Is there anything new in the works, or are these just a few special one-off performances? Mark: Short answer: remains to be seen, I guess. It’s certainly the case that now the negative pressure is gone, the joy is the central thing again. And although I’ve always been making sequences and melodies, it did bring me back into a work-on-a-thing-until-it-is-a-song ethic, which I quite like. Over the years, my main issue was that I couldn’t figure out how to bring our 80’s sound to today. But I think I’ve cracked that nut while preparing for Ombra. I’ve made some new music, but it’s not a consistent set. And maybe not all is P5 material. When there is a bunch of tracks that fit together, I’d love to release something again. And we’ve been talking about releasing a “Jerry” archive EP for years now. First with Death of Rave, but those talks ended alas. And now we’re figuring out how to release it ourselves. We have the original Luc Van Acker mix, my 2025 remix that mainly ups the punch, we have a demo that’s quite interesting and we have Silent Servant’s remix which was never released and has become stuff of legend.  Jo: Last year, a “Jerry” remix by Andi Harriman was included in one of Curse’s Next Wave Acid Punx Records. I think that brought us to a new crowd, too. Q: I can imagine that being back on stage after more than 35 years must have been a very special feeling. How did you prepare for that, both technically and emotionally? And how did you experience those performances yourselves? Mark: There were three months between the agreement with Ombra and the festival date, of which I was on holiday most of the first month. That left two months to prepare. About half of that went into figuring out how to do it in the first place. We’ve never travelled with gear on an airplane. And we surely weren’t bringing the fragile old gear. So, what gear would we use? I had to research how to do a complete live set in one Live set. And how to keep that ‘live’ enough. How would we output? Multi-out or one stereo mixdown? And what about visuals? We always tried to use video and projection. But the last time we did that on a stage, it was portable tube tv’s with VHS tapes and slide projectors. Today there’s ways to really sync video and audio. But how? Again, more research and learning.  In the end, we had one Mac with the Live session, with 8 synth and sample tracks, 8 drum tracks, a SMPTE time code track and a couple of Sysex tracks. The SMPTE connected to a second Mac with Resolume Arena software and a Komplete Kontrol setup with basically Kontakt resamples of the original S-50 and W-30 samples. Everything controlled with Push, two Faderfox controllers, two AKAI controllers and some pedals.  Jo: We did have access to the BELGIE venues, so we were able to do a couple of PA system repetitions. That helped us gain confidence for the Ombra show, last December (2025). And more importantly, it helped us find the joy in playing again. Gradually the show got in shape. But it’s a fact there was no time to do a lot of new music, or to rework some of the early, unreleased material. In the days, we had all the analog gear lined up and we experimented together. Now it was more of a reclusive thing, with Mark working on his Macs. We tested the progress on the PA, and I gave feedback. Which lead to more work for Mark. Our lives simply don’t allow for the experimentation of the past. I’m quite sorry about that evolution. Mark: There was so little time to prepare, there was hardly any time to feel anything, really. It was all about being ready in time. For me, the emotions came after the show. And I still feel them today. Q: With all the experience and wisdom you’ve accumulated since then, what advice would you give to the younger versions of yourselves who started making music in the ’80s? Mark: Work harder on your music. Take more time for it. And above all: finish tracks. Come to think of it, the advice still holds. Jo: Have fun, and remain impulsive, with life as your guide. I don’t like the ‘work’ verb of it too much. It’s not how we initially made music, nor how it can grow still. Our Barcelona experience showed us how our approach connected with a colorful contemporary audience. That adrenaline stayed high for months. If only for that, I wouldn’t mind doing more shows now.
items._genre: electro / EBM / industrial / underground electronic
items._cn_summary: 本文是对比利时地下电子乐队Philadelphia Five的回顾性访谈。文章追溯了该组合在上世纪八十年代末比利时Electro/EBM场景中的位置，将其置于Front 242、The Neon Judgement等著名乐队谱系中加以比较，并指出他们的声音虽同属地下电子范畴，却较少冷峻严肃，融入了幽默甚至自嘲元素，封面翻唱Boney M即为佐证。访谈由Side-Line杂志记者发起，经忠实读者牵线促成，内容覆盖乐队的创作背景、成员早年音乐根源（从Woodstock到Punk再到Tuxedomoon），以及他们与KK Records厂牌之间不愉快的合作经历。作者明确表达了对这支被低估乐队的敬意和感谢，并提及乐队近年在Ombra Festival和BIM Festival的演出，表明其音乐影响仍在延续。整体是一篇面向地下电子乐迷的专访，缺乏对具体声音设计或作品细节的深入分析。

items.body: Da Punch is the fourth album from the Parisian project Krystal System. ‘Bonnie’ and ‘N°7’ are joined by a new member, bassist ‘Phi’, who had already appeared on the EP preceding the album. Remarkably, this is their first full-length release since 2013. On ‘Da Punch’, Krystal System takes a critical look at society and interpersonal relationships, resulting in a collection of 13 tracks. I’ve always had a soft spot for Krystal System because, to me, they sound like a big ‘f*** you’ to all those bands that simply keep repeating themselves, gradually getting lost in a lack of creativity. Krystal System continues along its established path, delivering uncompromising compositions that blend guitar and electronics into an Electro-Post-Punk sound, driven by Bonnie’s passionate vocals. She sometimes sings in her native French, but most of the tracks are performed in English, delivered with that unmistakable and rather sexy French accent. N°7 also takes the microphone, providing a nice counterbalance to the female vocals and occasionally resulting in a duet. The songs are varied and, as mentioned, uncompromising. Their cover of Front 242’s “Headhunter” is a great example. Rather than simply copying the original—which would be sacrilege—they give it their own interpretation, and it really works. There are other, even stronger tracks to discover, with Krystal System occasionally channelling Rammstein-like guitar riffs and Depeche Mode-style melodies, while still remaining firmly rooted in their own sound. That’s what I call a modern Punk attitude, and it really appeals to me. Krystal System will need to put themselves back on the map for a wider audience, but music lovers who already know the band will simply be delighted to see them return with such a cool album. (Rating:8). Listen to “A World That Is Yours”: A World That Is Yours by Krystal System About Krystal System Krystal System started in Paris, France, in April 2006 under the name Krystal. The founding duo was Bonnie on vocals and guitar and N°7 (also stylized as Seven) on vocals, synths, and programming. A first demo, “Demain n’existe pas,” came before the project gained early exposure through the 2007 International Cravefest Video Awards and concerts in France and Switzerland. Around 2007 the duo signed to Belgian label Alfa Matrix and adopted the name Krystal System. Their debut album, “Underground,” followed on November 14, 2008, then the seven-track EP “Underground: VooDoo Night Sessions” on November 27, 2009, “Nuclear” on June 17, 2011, and “Rage” on March 15, 2013. Krystal System returned in 2025 with the “Éclats Rouges” EP, its first studio release since “Rage” and its first with bassist φ (Phi), expanding the lineup to a trio. “Da Punch,” the fourth Krystal System album, followed on June 26, 2026, again with the trio of Bonnie, N°7, and Phi. The 13-track release was made available digitally via Bandcamp and on CD through the Alfa Matrix Store, whose edition adds two bonus tracks, “Newclear Winter” and a 2025 version of the track. The album also includes a cover of a Front 242 song, “Headhunter.”
items._genre: electro-post-punk / industrial / EBM
items._cn_summary: Krystal System 来自巴黎，这是他们自2013年以来的首张全长专辑，阵容扩展为三人。新专辑收录13首作品，延续了将电吉他与电子合成器融合的路线，风格介于Post-Punk与Electro之间。Bonnie的女声时而用法语时而用英语演唱，带有明显的法式口音，与N°7的男声形成对位。对Front 242名曲的重新诠释体现了乐队的改编功力，吉他riff偶有Rammstein式的力量感，旋律则借鉴了Depeche Mode式的电子流行写法。整体保持不妥协的态度，未曾随波逐流，作品多样性较高且忠于自身美学。作为Alfa Matrix厂牌旗下的独立发行，在暗潮与工业电子交叉地带保持了扎实的辨识度，但未展现出突破性的实验意图或声音设计层面的创新。

items.body: DUKE ELLINGTON & JOHN COLTRANE - s/t (Impulse!, 1963) By Ferruccio Martinotti Sunday morning. We weren't even looking through Trane’s records, we already had a clear plan for the centenary. Then we spotted it. Or rather, it was almost as if IT was looking at us. There it was, humble and elusive amidst some truly gigantic "neighbors": “Duke Ellington & John Coltrane”. When a title says it all. How long had it been since it last took a spin on the turntable? A long, long time. So, we not only dusted it off, rescuing it from obscurity and oblivion but also cast it as the star of our own humble contribution to the Coltrane forum’s tribute. A quick preamble. Our favorite Trane is the one who burned all his bridges behind and embarked on the Path of Spiritual Ascension alongside Alice, Pharoah, Garrison, and Ali: for us, THIS is John’s definitive group. Since we are certain that our colleagues will, as usual, handle albums like ‘Interstellar Space”, “Olatunji”, “Live in Japan” et al, with the utmost mastery, we opted for a record you won’t find on "100 all-time best" playlists or among the essential albums by either Duke or Trane, yet one that is nonetheless deeply compelling. First things first: when and how did this encounter (the only one, if we’re not mistaken) between two of the greatest musicians of all time take place? The date: September 26, 1962. The setting: Rudy Van Gelder’s Studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, a place so legendary that, like Atlantis, one wonders if it ever truly existed. The mastermind: Bob Thiele, a producer at Impulse! The Maestri arrived at the meeting from different trajectories, not just in terms of age, but artistically as well. Duke, at 63, as the old king of the jungle, having already changed the course of music history in the 1920s and 30s, he wanted to show the "young lions" that the time to end up in the zoo hadn't arrived just yet. And judging by the extraordinary “Money Jungle”, recorded right some weeks earlier along with Max Roach and Charles Mingus, he had every right to feel that way. Trane, meanwhile, aged 35, was in a transitional phase. Leading one of jazz’s most sensational lineups ever (Jones, Garrison, Tyner), he had just released his first album for Impulse! in 1962, a record where modal structures were handled sublimely, yet he had not entirely cut ties with a more “mainstream” approach to his music (though, given the musical context, quotation marks are essential here!). It was as if, mid-journey, he had paused to catch his breath and look back one last time, before lighting the fuse and blowing everything wide open. The two arrived at the studio bringing their respective rhythm sections: Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones for Coltrane; Aaron Bell and Sam Woodyard from Ellington’s orchestra. To glimpse a moment of that historic occasion, we can turn to bassist John Lamb, who was present that day: “There was no music on that whole date. Nobody had a chart. We came in and we were standing there, waiting to see what would have happen. Trane would go and sit on the piano bench with Duke. They didn’t talk but Duke would be singing and Trane would go. Then, after they did that for a few minutes, they got up. Trane would go to his microphone, Duke would start playing and the rhythm section, we had to do for ourselves, you know. That’s it. He didn’t even tell you the key. He could communicate without words and Trane could hear it.” The eight-hour session yielded seven tracks: “In a Sentimental Mood”, “Take The Coltrane” and “Stevie” (two sketches composed right there in the studio), “Angelica” and “The Feeling of Jazz” by Ellington; Billy Strayhorn’s “My Little Brown Book”; and Coltrane’s “Big Nick,” a tribute to tenor saxophonist Big Nick Nicholas. At work here are two living legends who set out not to change history, but simply to experience, with mutual respect and admiration, the intimate joy of music. No overbearing displays, no pointless academic showing-off or gratuitous virtuosity. Pure Magic. Even Elvin Jones puts down the sticks of dynamite and picks up the brushes. It is a "Sunday Morning Record", relaxed, atmospheric, and straightforward, reminding us that in our constant search for the ultimate, mind-blowing thrill (which, by definition, is NEVER the last one), we often lose sight of the wonder of simplicity. This is the perfect album to set that right. Let us leave the final word on this experience to Trane: “I was really honored to have the opportunity of working with Duke. It was a wonderful experience. He has set standards I haven’t caught up with yet. I would have liked to have worked over all those numbers again, but I guess the performances wouldn’t have had the same spontaneity. And they mightn’t have been any better.” May the Journey be light for you, dear John. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: jazz / modal jazz / hard bop / mainstream jazz
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦于1963年Impulse!厂牌发行的《Duke Ellington & John Coltrane》专辑，作为Coltrane百年诞辰致敬系列的一部分。文章描述了1962年9月26日在Rudy Van Gelder传奇录音室中，两位爵士巨匠的唯一一次录音合作。评论者明确表示自己更偏爱Coltrane与Alice Coltrane、Pharoah Sanders等人合作的自由即兴与灵性探索阶段，但这张专辑则展现了一个过渡期的Coltrane——在彻底突破之前，他仍保留着与更主流爵士语汇的关联。Ellington以63岁高龄带来成熟老练的作曲功底，Coltrane的四人经典节奏组与Ellington乐队的节奏组同场竞技，全程无谱即兴。乐评指出专辑并非两张大师各自代表作的集锦，而是真正发生音乐对话的稀有文献，对理解两位艺术家交汇时刻具有独特价值。

items.album: SOPHYA BACCINI Sophya Baccini's Aradia: Runnin' with the Wolves (Rock Progressivo Italiano, 2023)
items.excerpt: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Sophya Baccini is no stranger to the world of prog rock. After contributing to the album *Palepolitana* by the veterans of Osanna in 2015, then reviving her former band Presence for a sixth studio album?the unclassifiable *Masters and Following*, an unlikely encounter between Keith Emerson's *Inferno* (1980) and Lacrimosa's *Inferno* (1995)?and before playing a major role in a seemingly endless (3 jam-packed CDs) tribute to Bowie/Bolan?which also featured Fran
items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Sophya Baccini is no stranger to the world of prog rock. After contributing to the album *Palepolitana* by the veterans of Osanna in 2015, then reviving her former band Presence for a sixth studio album?the unclassifiable *Masters and Following*, an unlikely encounter between Keith Emerson's *Inferno* (1980) and Lacrimosa's *Inferno* (1995)?and before playing a major role in a seemingly endless (3 jam-packed CDs) tribute to Bowie/Bolan?which also featured Franck Carducci?Sophya (originally named Sofia, then Sophia) gave us an update in 2023, both on stage (performing covers of classics by Yes and Kate Bush, for example) and in the studio with *Animatesi*, released in January?a more intimate album than usual, featuring Sophya alone at the piano. And in the second half of 2023, she's finally back with an album by Aradia, her all-female band equally possessed by the spirit of baroque progressive rock. Unlike *Big Red Dragon*, her previous album, *Runnin' with the Wolves* doesn't feature a lineup of prestigious guest artists. Sophya and her rousing piano are backed by a formidable all-female lineup: Marilena on keyboards, Francesca on violin, Sonia on guitar and saxophone, Anais on bass, and Chiara on drums?a rarity in the world of prog that's worth noting, especially since this testosterone-free lineup gives this baroque RPI an uncommon elegance. Nevertheless, we find here the signature style that Sophya has been developing for years, both as a solo artist and with Presence?a sort of decadent, theatrical rock that owes a great deal to the Bowie of the '70s, to Sparks (she even covered "This Town Ain't Big Enough for Both of Us" on Presence's latest album), to Kurt Weill and the most tender, romantic Kate Bush, without ever straying far from Italian symphonic prog in the vein of Banco. It's a curious combination that warrants a detailed description of the seven tracks that make up this intriguing *Runnin' with the Wolves*. More than once or twice, more than three or four times?let's say half a dozen times?I've tried to put into words what came to mind while listening to these melancholic waltzes, these sophisticated arrangements, these progressive lullabies, and the highly elaborate structure of the lengthy "Continua" (9:17), but it was a lost cause. I couldn't write without letting go of the brakes on my imagination without stumbling over every syllable. Because *Runnin' with the Wolves* is an album that can't be described but must be listened to endlesslyAt a time when Taylor Swift's sanitized, slightly WASP-ish pop sells millions of copies worldwide and racks up billions of views on YouTube?all while scrupulously adhering to the "rule of three": no more than three chords, no more than three notes in the melody, and no more than three beats in the rhythm (and often only two)?does music as genuinely warm and colorful as Sophya Baccini's have a place in this grand burlesque spectacle that means so much to all of us: modern music? Yes, but only a small spot at the very back of the room, perhaps insufficiently but proudly illuminated by media outlets like this one. So let's shine a light on it?let's be enlightening and enlightened?in the hope of encouraging as many people as possible to listen closely to this entirely female, one-of-a-kind prog band.
items._genre: baroque prog / RPI / art rock / theatrical rock
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由全女性阵容演绎意大利巴洛克前卫摇滚，延续了Sophya Baccini一贯的戏剧化颓废风格。编曲融合了七十年代Bowie的华丽摇滚质感、Sparks的怪诞优雅、Kurt Weill的剧场气质与Kate Bush的浪漫细腻，同时扎根于Banco式的交响前卫框架。钢琴主导的架构配合小提琴、键盘、吉他与萨克斯的层次铺陈，七首曲目呈现抑郁圆舞曲式的氛围与精密复杂的结构，长篇曲目"Continua"超过九分钟，层层递进。乐评指出这张作品难以用文字概括，需要反复聆听才能体会其音乐逻辑：一种介于前卫摇篮曲与巴洛克仪式之间的声响世界，既保留了意大利前卫摇滚的古典气质，又融入了英式艺术摇滚的感性表达。

items.body: Review by CeeJayGee — I first discovered The Tangent 15 years ago, but it took me another couple of years to realise how good their music is. For a few years they were one of a handful of bands that I would call my favourites. The quality of the albums over the last few years has been so high that I would now say The Tangent is my favourite and most listened to band. I also appreciate being able to engage with Andie Tillison via social media. After I commented on the quality of this year's Po90 release, aftersometimelater, saying that it deserved to be more heavily marketed to raise its profile, Andie asked me whether I would like to hear some of the forthcoming album, Was. I jumped at the opportunity. I thought I would hear just a couple of tracks but over several weeks I was able to listen to and comment on the entire album. The album tells Andie's story through the music and the events that have shaped his own musical career. You could call it autobiographical. I don't believe anyone has attempted this previously and the purpose of the album has clearly inspired Andie to create some wonderful melodies.The first track I heard was the title track which I found immediately likeable and kept playing on repeat. I loved the simplicity of the riff which develops through the 22 minutes of the track. I couldn't stop playing it after the first listen. I then heard the Was Suite which at over 53 minutes is structured as six named segments that flow perfectly from one to another on the album. In classical music they would be called movements. When I first heard it, it was a single track. This is a largely instrumental piece and my past interest in classical music, and my love of rock and jazz fusion, makes this compulsive listening. The final segment, titled "Let Me Sing", is Andie sharing how he communicates through his music and his messages through poetic lyrics. It is a powerful conclusion which finishes with an inspirational speaker advising a young audience how to have good lives. I then heard Was Not, which Andie indicated to me was his favourite. This is another complex 20 minute plus and certainly matches Was and the Suite in terms of quality. The track opens with Andie's impressions of World War II formed from what he learned from the people who lived through and survived it, and the many films and TV series which his family watched together in his youth. I am a bit older than Andie, but I can empathise with this totally. The track develops with memories of further events and the hope that the World would learn from its past mistakes. He continues that the horrors we all see through the media seem to make us numb and he concludes with a very personal memory of his father in a nursing home. It is an extraordinary piece. The underlying themes and melodies are most enjoyable, but the piece is dominated by the message. For me, these are three standout pieces of music and these tracks are destined to be classics. The album also includes Follow The River plus four bonus tracks (two of which are around 20 minutes long) which are all enjoyable. I have little doubt that this will be my favourite 2026 album and it is likely to end up being my favourite album by The Tangent (so far).
items._genre: eclectic prog / progressive rock / jazz fusion / classical influence
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以自传体叙事为主轴，乐手通过音乐讲述个人经历与职业生涯的塑造过程。标题曲以简洁的riff发展为22分钟的渐进结构，Was Suite以六个乐章式的段落串联起超过53分钟的器乐叙事，融合古典音乐、摇滚与爵士融合的语汇。Was Not一曲以二战记忆为切入点，结合家庭观影经历与个人回忆，最终以父亲在养老院的私人画面作结。整体制作注重旋律性与情感传达，器乐编排复杂但服务于叙事目的。评论者因长期关注该乐队并提前试听全专，强调三首核心曲目具有经典潜力。专辑在旋律记忆点与主题深度之间取得平衡，适合偏爱长篇器乐叙事与个人化表达的听众。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the many one and done acts that emerged in Germany's fertile Krautrock scene actually lastedfrom 1973 when it formed in Bottrop until the band folded in 1980. While only releasing one album,1975's BROKEN DOOR, the band went through many lineup changes with only one version of the bandmanaging to record and release something but even though a single album was recorded and set tovinyl, it was produced in such low numbers that it was virtually forgotten shortly after its releasealthough the band did frequent the live circuits for its entire run. Luckily BROKEN DOOR was rescuedby the Garden of Delights label and has emerged as one of those unexpected gems that was almostcompletely lost to history.With a rather contradictory band name juxtaposed to a disheartening album title, PROSPER wassomewhat unique and whereas some German prog was not Krautrock and not all Krautrock wasprogressive, PROSPER found the nice in-between zone that allowed the headier atmospheric texturesand spaciness of the koschmische sounds exist in full space rock mode all the while offering anabundance of virtuosic instrumental moments mostly courtesy of guitarist Evert Brettschneider whowas concurrently active in the jazz fusion group Contract Trio. Not surprisingly some of thisjazziness seeped into PROSPER which works surprisingly well. Add some King Crimson grit to the mixand you're in for a real treat with this one.The album is primarily instrumental dishing out a multitude of space rock-tinged motifs laced withmoments of progressive rock heft and jazzy accouterments. The band was a five-piece but implementeda diverse array of guitar tones (both acoustic and electric) as well as a plethora of keys rangingfrom the Fender Rhodes and Mini-Moog to mellotrons and other electronic effects however the thumpingbass grooves clearly point to Amon Dull II's heady mix of kosmische kraftiness. The album featuredeight tracks which range from softer contemplative space rock to more jazz-fueled prog. The opening"Beginning" offers a nice rotisserie of all the styles on the menu and elegantly passes the batonfrom one genre shift to another. The band's dexterity in handling the instrumentation allows thealbum to take on a more epic feel as opposed to many Kraut acts that were simply going for theescapist approach.While the album is fairly uniform in its feel, the mid-album clunker "Your Country" sounds woefullyout of place with its country rock style that wouldn't have sounded out of place on an album fromThe Band and although competently performed somewhat derails the momentum of the album's continuityhowever the surrounding material is strong enough to allow the listener to merely shrug it off assome kind of unfortunate anomaly. Overall PROSPER's debut release is indeed a true gem that took thebest aspects of the varying Krautrock and prog styles of the era and seamlessly agglutinated it allinto a cohesive sound of its own right. This is indeed a band that should've released another albumor two before evaporating into the 1980s but like many bands of the day, we're actually lucky toeven have the opportunity to experience this one once rare and unknown band's sole artifact.
items._genre: krautrock / space rock / jazz fusion / progressive rock
items._cn_summary: 1975年德国Krautrock场景中仅存一张录音室的PROSPER乐队专辑《Broken Door》，由Garden of Delights小厂牌重新发行得以重见天日。专辑以器乐演奏为主，融合太空摇滚的氛围纹理与宇宙感的迷幻音景，同时融入大量爵士融合元素，主要由吉他手Evert Brettschneider贡献。五人编制运用了丰富的电吉他与木吉他音色，加上Fender Rhodes、Minimoog、mellotron等多种键盘与电子音效，贝斯线条带有Amon Düül II式的宇宙感律动。八首曲目在柔美沉思的太空摇滚与爵士化前卫摇滚之间流转，开篇曲作为全专辑风格的缩影，在多种风格转换间自然衔接。唯一的中段曲目《Your Country》以乡村摇滚风格显得格格不入，但整体器乐驾驭能力使专辑呈现出超越多数同期Krautrock乐队的史诗感。

items.body: Cabaret Voltaire have released the remastered single version of “Here To Go“, the second of the two UK chart singles from their 1987 album “CODE”, ahead of its remastered reissue on 9 October via Mute. The track follows the 7-inch version of “Don’t Argue“, shared from the same reissue in August. “CODE” was Cabaret Voltaire’s eighth studio album and the record that followed Richard H Kirk and Stephen Mallinder’s move to EMI, both singles breaking the UK Official Singles Chart on the album’s original release. Speaking in the reissue’s new sleeve notes, Mallinder describes the record as a document of its moment: “This album shows a very interesting moment in time where we were moving into a technological world. Probably more than anything else Richard and I made together, CODE was a political record that we didn’t have to directly articulate as political, mostly because of what was going on in the background at that time.” Out of print for years, the reissue arrives on limited “CODIFIED” marble vinyl and as a triple CD set, the CD edition adding two discs of period remixes and previously unreleased mixes pulled from the archive. Guest musicians on the original sessions included saxophonist Simeon Lister, bassist Mark Brydon of Chakk and Bill Nelson of Be-Bop Deluxe; the album was recorded at the band’s own Western Works studio in Sheffield with Adrian Sherwood joining for pre-production before mixing moved to Red Bus in London. Denis Blackman, who has mastered or remastered every Cabaret Voltaire album for more than 20 years, handled the remaster. Work on the reissue began in 2019 with Kirk and was completed after his death using his notes, in consultation with Mallinder and Kirk’s estate. ‘CODE’ tracklist CODE vinyl (cat. CABS27): Don’t Argue Sex, Money, Freaks Thank You America Here To Go Trouble (Won’t Stop) White Car No One Here Life Slips By Code The triple CD (cat. CABS27CD) carries the same nine tracks on disc one, followed by two further discs of remixes, including the John Robie dub of “Thank You America” already shared when Mute announced the reissue, and the 7-inch version of “Don’t Argue”. Cabaret Voltaire’s final tour dates Stephen Mallinder and Chris Watson close the run marking 50 years since the band’s first performance. I Speak Machine supports the North American shows, Gazelle Twin most of the UK dates and Fader the two south-west English shows. 7 October – Dublin (Ireland), The Academy 8 October – Belfast (UK), Limelight 10 October – Birmingham (UK), Town Hall, with Gazelle Twin 11 October – Liverpool (UK), Arts Club, with Gazelle Twin – sold out 13 October – Nottingham (UK), The Palais, with Gazelle Twin 14 October – Cardiff (UK), The Globe, with Fader 15 October – Bath (UK), Forum, with Fader 17 October – Newcastle (UK), Boiler Shop, with Gazelle Twin 18 October – Glasgow (UK), Barrowland, with Gazelle Twin 19 October – Manchester (UK), Albert Hall, with Gazelle Twin 21 October – Brighton (UK), Chalk, with Gazelle Twin 22 October – London (UK), Roundhouse, with Gazelle Twin – sold out 25 October – Sheffield (UK), Octagon, with Gazelle Twin – sold out About Cabaret Voltaire Cabaret Voltaire formed in Sheffield in 1973 around Richard H Kirk, Stephen Mallinder and Chris Watson. Watson left in 1981; Kirk and Mallinder continued as a duo, signing to EMI and issuing “CODE” in 1987, the album behind their two UK chart singles, “Don’t Argue” and “Here To Go”. The pair wound the project down in 1994. Kirk later continued alone, performing at Berlin’s Atonal festival in 2014 and releasing “Shadow of Fear”, “BN9Drone” and “Dekadrone” across 2020 and 2021, before his death in autumn 2021. Mallinder and Watson returned to the stage in 2025 for the 50th-anniversary run, which included a Roundhouse date announced for 2026 and continued this year around the live album “But What Time Is It Really?“, from which the duo also shared a live version of “Yashar”. The “CODE” reissue lands in the final weeks of that tour, following “Here To Go” onto the same stages that first carried it in 1987.

items._cn_summary: 本文并非传统意义上的乐评，而是一则关于Cabaret Voltaire 1987年专辑《CODE》再版发行的综合资讯。文章介绍了"Here To Go"单曲混音版的释出、再版格式（大理石黑胶与三碟CD套装）、幕后制作人员（包括客座乐手Bill Nelson、Simeon Lister及混音师Adrian Sherwood的参与），以及主创Stephen Mallinder关于该专辑时代背景的回顾性陈述。文章还列出了巡演日程信息。作为工业电子与后朋克的先驱者，Cabaret Voltaire此次再版提供了大量未发行混音与同期remix，对于该领域爱好者具有档案价值。整体内容偏向新闻发布性质，缺乏深入的乐评分析或音乐评论文字。

items.body: Deep utterances and smoky melodies fill the old courtyards of Jozef Van Wissem’s music. On Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back (Consouling Sounds), the lute’s spidery melodies appear as finely woven webs, echoing into the present from the distant past. Something is brewing. An explosive beat rocks the medieval sound to its core, less a queasy shake and more like a 7.o earthquake. The misty and quietly revolutionary tones carry the ill weight of death. The melodies themselves are almost like the Black Death, spreading throughout the eastern European townships of the album and going door-to-door, knocking lightly like a strange, dark-coated preacher – ‘you will come with me now’, it says – as the sickening fog leaves behind nothing but stark, quiet streets and stained doors, a field of hastily-painted crosses traced along both sides. Clammy-faced inhabitants are locked inside otherwise empty rooms, and a row of filled tombs line the music, track by track. There is something incredibly earthy to the sound, like century-old soil. Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back takes its inspiration from a painting by Belgian artist Cindy Wright (her painting is the one on the cover). Things are delicate here, as delicate and as temporary as a note on a quivering string before it fades into permanent silence, into its flame-streaked sunset, ultimately moving into the death of itself and its subsequent absorption into the earth and air. Nothing lasts forever, and the skull on the cover testifies to that. Van Wissem’s music plucks a very distinct chord. The notes are splayed out like an ancient victim on a medieval rack, but there’s more of an emphasis on pleasure rather than on pain, with echoing vocals calling out from a cold, lantern-lit chamber, soaking into the cold slabs of stone, and the masterful playing of the lute ringing through the draughty corridors. At other times, the lute appears stately and dignified, resplendent in a magnificent, proud set of robes. But the sparse arrangement, as well as the concentrated focus on one instrument, ensures that beneath the robed appearance there lies a body that’s thin bordering on the anorexic or even the skeletal, despite a flurry of faster passages that seem to run at quite a pace and with a good deal of urgency. The notes are still as narrow as a spindle, and that’s just a characteristic of the lute. Pockets of light are able to shine weakly out from the brighter tracks, offering a pale, stained-glass-window light. There are other reinterpretations of death here, too: a death of a nation as the British PM makes a suicidal statement. But the rose is still beautiful even as it dies. The future has and always will be an uncertain unknown, but willingly jumping off the edge without first looking down or checking to see where you’re going seems to be neither a sane nor reasonable course of action. Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back revels in its uncertainty and in its transient nature. It began as dust, and to dust it returns. www.consouling.be
items._genre: lute music / medieval / dark folk / experimental
items._cn_summary: Jozef Van Wissem 的鲁特琴独奏专辑以中世纪为底色，旋律如蛛网般细密而幽深，弥漫着黑色死亡般的意象与沉重氛围。评论以浓烈的死亡美学贯穿全文，将琴声比作敲门的瘟疫使者、街巷中来不及绘完的十字墓碑，强调其脆弱而短暂、如火焰般的瞬时美感。编曲极度稀疏，聚焦单一乐器，使音色在庄严华服下显露出近乎骨瘦的骨架，偶尔出现的急促段落带来紧迫感。专辑封面来自比利时艺术家 Cindy Wright 的画作，呼应了关于国家之死与时代不确定性的主题。整体在古老鲁特琴传统之上叠加了实验性的暗黑叙事与死亡哲学，在暗潮、当代古典与世界音乐的交界处形成了独特的冥想空间。

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. Find the artist online. Sara Serpa - Encounters and Collisions (Review) Karine Polwart- Laws of Motion (Review) Live in the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, 2025

items._cn_summary: 这是一张以人声与钢琴为核心的专辑，源于艺术家在爱丁堡皇家植物园的驻留项目。钢琴手Dave Milligan的演奏克制而富有共情，与Karine Polwart温暖、富有同情心的嗓音共同构建出亲密的氛围。制作人兼声音设计师Pippa Murphy贡献了审慎的声景设计，为人声与钢琴为主的简约编排增添了层次。专辑围绕一棵2021年被砍伐的棕榈树展开——这颗树曾被误认了两百年，最终种子将萌发新苗。作品将树木的故事延伸为对自然、历史与人自身记忆的沉思，声音朴素却具有史诗般的纵深。文字与音乐中反复出现的短语如同记忆锚点，让听众从旁观者变为参与者。整体风格扎根苏格兰，却以全球视野审视万物之间的联结，是民谣与声音艺术、环境叙事结合的跨界作品。

items._genre: contemporary classical / chamber / experimental jazz / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张作品是作曲家大卫·朱宾斯基为普瑞斯姆四重奏「释放你内在作曲家」系列委约创作的一首短篇室内乐作品，2025年11月在费城免费图书馆首演。演奏阵容包括萨克斯四重奏、人声（厄休拉·拉克尔）、打击乐（小泰肖恩·索雷）和小提琴（卡洛斯·圣地亚哥），由作曲家与四位合作者共同完成编曲与演绎。乐评指出作品在不到四分钟内完成从粗粝到抒情的往返，展现出力度与精致并存的气质。文末仅做简介推荐，未深入剖析配器手法或结构逻辑，信息密度有限。整体属于当代古典与即兴跨界范畴，对偏好先锋与融合语汇的听众具有吸引力，但文本更像导赏引介而非深度评论。

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?
items.label: Go' Danish Folk Music
items._genre: Nordic folk / traditional / experimental folk
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自丹麦三人的首张数字EP，包含五首作品，以北欧传统民乐为基底。主唱Mia Guldhammer嗓音低沉而富有穿透力，是乐评中最受推崇的核心元素。乐曲大量使用口簧琴、风笛、扬琴、长笛和弦乐等传统或古朴乐器，营造出古老、略带粗糙的氛围。唯一的原创曲目来自乐队成员Morten Musicas，名为《Nordgård》，带有持续推进感的节奏律动。传统民谣《Agnete Of Bjergmanden》在扬琴的衬托下展现细腻层次，而纯器乐曲目《Ormsö》将口簧琴与长笛、弦乐交织，产生怪异的离调张力。整张EP呈现出成熟而克制的风格，以传统为根基但在音色编排上带有一定实验色彩。乐评将其定位为一次有力的亮相，期待乐队未来在完整专辑中展现更多可能。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由瑞典小提琴手与两位挪威乐手组成的跨国三重奏专辑，以室内乐般的对话方式重新诠释斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲素材。小提琴、竖笛（sølfløyte）与鼓的组合将传统旋律剥离为碎片化的即兴纹理，强调音乐中潜在的黑暗与神秘意味。正如乐评所指出的，乐手刻意模糊了舞曲与沉思性聆听体验之间的边界——这不是适合舞蹈的伴奏，而是对民间音乐隐藏可能性的深层探索。专辑选择以挪威塞特斯达尔河谷的《Fossgrimen》开篇，呼应民间传说中瀑布精灵赋予小提琴手技艺的神话叙事，为整张作品奠定了不安而内省的氛围基调。

items.body: Cuatro Piraguas started “La Cumbia del Jardinero” after a sleepless night and a small gardening episode at Villa Plagwitz in Leipzig, which suits a debut album called En vela, Spanish for a night spent awake. The quartet take their name from the dugout canoes of Latin America and the Caribbean, and work across Afro-Peruvian rhythm, Colombian Caribbean folklore and the music of Venezuela and Brazil. Celia Regina sings and plays cuatro, with Mauricio Vivas on accordion, guitar and cuatro, Thomas Campbell Tyler on bass and Felix Zehdnicker on percussion. A year of live shows shaped the song, and the recording with their friend Max Gruener adds clarinet and trombone from Eldar Tsalikov and Marleen Dahms, plus backing vocals from friends. The band name two Colombian influences: Totó la Momposina, the singer from the river island of Mompox who died in May aged 85, and Cali-born songwriter Marta Gómez. The verses fill a gardener’s morning with small chores done with affection: coffee at the window, water against a dry spell, an ear for what each plant has to say. The chorus switches to labour, alternating between a gardener who works all day and a wheelbarrow that keeps rolling. The band read that routine as a picture of their own debut: gardens and records both take time and care before anything flowers. En vela is due this autumn, and vinyl, CD and download pre-orders run through their crowdfunding page until 27 September. Two nights before it closes, they play a free gig at Kulturbar froelich & herrlich, beneath Leipzig’s Westflügel puppet theatre on Friday 25 September. items._cn_summary: Cuatro Piraguas 是一支以拉丁美洲独木舟命名的四重奏，首张专辑《En vela》源自一次失眠后的清晨园艺灵感。他们将非洲秘鲁节奏、哥伦比亚加勒比民俗音乐以及委内瑞拉、巴西的音乐元素交织融合，主唱 Celia Regina 演奏委内瑞拉四弦琴，配以手风琴、贝斯与打击乐。单曲《La Cumbia del Jardinero》以园丁的晨间琐事构建叙事，歌词描绘窗边的咖啡、为干旱浇水、倾听每株植物的声音，副歌转向劳作主题，交替呈现整天劳作的园丁与不停滚动的手推车。乐队将这一日常视为自身首张专辑的隐喻：花园与唱片都需要时间与照料才能绽放。录音由好友 Max Gruener 操刀，加入单簧管与长号，呈现温暖而内省的拉丁民俗气质。
